AI.method: Compares single-model signals (confidence, logit margin, attention entropy) against cross-version signals (output KL divergence, likelihood drift, token-level KL, representation drift) using a unified added-value test to isolate each signal's gain over a confidence baseline. Evaluates across six benchmarks in three task families (multiple-choice QA, math reasoning, code generation) and six model update pairs.
AI.result: (1) Signal effectiveness is task-dependent: confidence strongest on MCQ and simpler math, while likelihood/KL signals give most frequent gains on harder math and code. (2) No signal is universally best across model updates. (3) Cross-version signals remain informative even when confidence fails, enabling a proof-of-concept selective fallback that routes high-risk samples back to the old model.
AI.conclusion: Different regression signals work best for different tasks and model updates, providing practitioners with task-level patterns to choose which signals to trust. Cross-version signals offer valuable information even without labels, supporting practical fallback mechanisms to mitigate regression risks in LLM updates.

title: Capacity-Dependent Effects of Data Selection for Reasoning
comment: Accepted to COLM 2026
summary: In reasoning supervised fine-tuning, candidate responses for the same instruction can differ substantially in how well they match the student's current distribution. Recent likelihood-based response selection methods suggest that responses closer to the student distribution provide more effective supervision, motivating the hypothesis that high-likelihood responses may generally be preferable for fine-tuning. In this paper, we revisit this intuition and show that the value of likelihood-based data selection depends critically on model capacity and training duration. Through controlled experiments on mathematical reasoning, using students ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters and supervision generated by stronger teacher models, we observe a clear \emph{capacity-dependent} ``{\color{SMALLCOLOR}\textbf{Fast-Fit}} / {\color{LARGECOLOR}\textbf{Slow-Gain}}'' pattern. High-likelihood data provides faster and more stable early improvements, especially for smaller models, but low-likelihood data becomes increasingly beneficial for larger models when training is allowed to continue longer. To explain this phenomenon, we analyze learning dynamics, showing that small models often fail to absorb low-likelihood supervision and instead fall into shallow or repetitive behaviors, while larger models are better able to move toward the teacher distribution under such data. We further provide a capacity-constrained theoretical view of distillation that clarifies how data difficulty, data span, and student capacity jointly govern transfer. Overall, our findings show that effective data selection for reasoning should be aware of model capacity and computing budget rather than based on a single universal preference for high-likelihood supervision.

AI.tldr: High-likelihood data works better for small models (fast fit), but low-likelihood data becomes beneficial for large models with longer training (slow gain), showing capacity-dependent data selection effects in reasoning fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the common intuition that high-likelihood responses are always better for supervised fine-tuning in reasoning tasks. Recent methods suggest responses closer to student distribution provide better supervision, but the authors question whether this holds universally across different model capacities and training durations.
AI.method: The authors conduct controlled experiments on mathematical reasoning using student models ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters, with supervision generated by stronger teacher models. They analyze learning dynamics and provide a capacity-constrained theoretical view of distillation that considers data difficulty, data span, and student capacity.
AI.result: They discover a clear "Fast-Fit/Slow-Gain" pattern: high-likelihood data provides faster and more stable early improvements (especially for small models), while low-likelihood data becomes increasingly beneficial for larger models with extended training. Small models struggle to absorb low-likelihood supervision and fall into shallow behaviors, while larger models can better move toward teacher distribution.
AI.conclusion: Effective data selection for reasoning should be capacity-aware and consider computing budget rather than following a universal preference for high-likelihood supervision. The value of likelihood-based data selection critically depends on model capacity and training duration.

title: Evaluating Agentic Learning Harness Capabilities Without Labels via the Scaling Hypothesis
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at CAMLIS 2025 (Conference on Applied Machine Learning for Information Security)
summary:
Agentic "Continual Learning Harnesses", systems that pair an LLM with retrieval or memory to improve from feedback without retraining, have shown growing value in cybersecurity. But their value is conventionally measured by gains against labeled benchmarks, an approach that often fails in operational security settings. Benchmark labels are scarce, stale, and unrepresentative, so a practitioner often cannot tell whether a given harness helps at all or which of two is better for their task. Traditional LLM-as-a-judge offers little signal because it is no stronger than the agent it evaluates, and distillation is unreliable on scarce, sporadic, and biased labels.
  We propose a framework for evaluating learning harnesses end-to-end without a labeled benchmark, grounded in the scaling hypothesis. A stronger teacher model provides sparsely sampled corrections to a smaller student with a continual learning harness. We score a harness by how much its student converges toward the teacher over time. Across security tasks, model families, and harness designs, we show that improvement relative to the teacher correlates with improvement relative to a held-out gold standard, validating teacher-relative lift as a proxy for true harness uplift when labels are absent. We further show that LLM-as-a-judge between similarly powered models yields no usable signal. These results suggest that a teacher-sized model can be improved through the same harness when humans provide the same kind of sparse, high-precision corrections.

AI.tldr: A framework for evaluating continual learning harnesses without labeled benchmarks by measuring how much a smaller student model converges toward a stronger teacher model over time through sparse corrections.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of agentic continual learning harnesses in cybersecurity relies on labeled benchmarks, which are scarce, stale, and unrepresentative. Traditional LLM-as-a-judge evaluation offers little signal, and distillation is unreliable on limited labels.
AI.method: Propose a teacher-student framework where a stronger teacher model provides sparsely sampled corrections to a smaller student with a continual learning harness. The harness is scored by measuring how much the student converges toward the teacher over time.
AI.result: Across security tasks, model families, and harness designs, improvement relative to the teacher correlates with improvement relative to a held-out gold standard. Teacher-relative lift serves as a proxy for true harness uplift when labels are absent. LLM-as-a-judge between similarly powered models yields no usable signal.
AI.conclusion: Teacher-relative evaluation provides a practical framework for assessing continual learning harnesses in operational security settings where labeled benchmarks are unavailable. A teacher-sized model could be improved through the same harness when humans provide similar sparse, high-precision corrections.

title: The Integer Alibi: Localizing Cross-Kernel Divergence in INT8-Quantized LLM Inference
comment: 10 pages (IEEEtran two-column), 4 figures, 4 tables. Pre-registered protocol with append-only amendments; measurement artifacts and per-run manifests with kernel-selection evidence are described in the artifact statement. Companion to arXiv:2608.11693
summary: Two GPU kernels implementing the same scaled INT8 GEMM interface are usually treated as interchangeable. We test that assumption: holding the checkpoint, prompts, hardware, inference engine, decoding, and quantization configuration fixed, we swap only the INT8 linear kernel (CUTLASS versus Triton) inside vLLM. At 1.7B each arm reproduces itself bit-for-bit across cold restarts, yet the arms agree on no sequence in any end-to-end comparison we ran (0/8, 0/16, and 0/64). What makes this more than a benchmark discrepancy is an integer alibi: for shared INT8 operands under a verified no-overflow bound, the INT32 dot product is exact and order-independent, so the accumulator cannot be the source of any difference. Feeding both kernels identical operands from every linear layer of Qwen3-1.7B and 8B (196 and 252 layers), we find bit-identical outputs under power-of-two scales, confirming a pinned prediction list 196/196 and 252/252 (pre-registered at 1.7B, pinned but not blind at 8B), and observed differences of at most one bfloat16 spacing under the checkpoints' real scales. This localizes the divergence to scale application and output rounding after the exact accumulator. Applied as a probe checkpoint, the same intervention restores end-to-end bitwise agreement (8/8 and 16/16 sequences). Cross-implementation FP8 GEMM shows a different signature: both the prevalence and the magnitude of differences grow with reduction depth, while the INT8 fraction stays at parts per million and within one spacing over a 64x range of K. Teacher-forced replay ties layers to tokens: flips concentrate at small logit margins, which predict flip risk with ROC-AUC 0.94 on 16,384 positions. We will release the pre-registration, per-layer predictions, manifests with kernel-selection evidence, and a conformance procedure that turns these controls into a concrete check for kernel interchangeability.

AI.tldr: INT8 GEMM kernels from different implementations (CUTLASS vs Triton) are not interchangeable despite identical interfaces, causing end-to-end sequence mismatches due to differences in scale application and rounding after exact integer accumulation.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the common assumption that GPU kernels implementing the same scaled INT8 GEMM interface are interchangeable. While the integer dot product is mathematically exact and order-independent, real-world kernel swaps cause sequence-level discrepancies in inference, motivating investigation into the true sources of divergence.
AI.method: Systematically compared CUTLASS and Triton INT8 GEMM kernels while holding everything else constant in vLLM. Verified no-overflow conditions to ensure integer dot products are exact. Tested with Qwen3-1.7B and 8B models across 196 and 252 layers. Used power-of-two scales to isolate differences and real checkpoint scales to measure divergence magnitude. Applied teacher-forced replay to analyze token-level effects.
AI.result: Found 0% sequence agreement between kernels despite bit-for-bit reproducibility within each kernel. Identified that divergence occurs during scale application and output rounding, not in the integer accumulation. Achieved 196/196 and 252/252 layer predictions confirmed under power-of-two scales. Differences were limited to at most one bfloat16 spacing under real scales. FP8 GEMM showed different error patterns growing with reduction depth, while INT8 errors stayed at ppm levels.
AI.conclusion: INT8 GEMM kernels are not interchangeable due to implementation differences in scale application and rounding, which can cause end-to-end sequence divergence. The paper provides a conformance procedure to test kernel interchangeability and will release tools to detect these subtle but significant differences.

title: SemPlan: Benchmarking Structured Semantic Planning for LLM-Based Queries over Enterprise Data
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Natural-language interfaces to enterprise data must translate underspecified requests into governed, executable behavior while controlling invalid queries, policy failures, cost, and nondeterminism. SemPlan Benchmark evaluates this architectural design space with a deterministic synthetic bilingual benchmark containing 1,800 cases in English and Brazilian Portuguese; 1,200 cases form the frozen scientific evaluation subset. Four architectures are compared under the same model configuration: direct SQL generation (A1), a bounded tool-agent baseline (A2), structured semantic-request generation followed by deterministic planning and execution (A3), and a clarification/stateful semantic-plan variant (A4). Across 4,800 primary records, answer correctness was low in absolute terms: 22.25% for A1, 22.58% for A2, 25.67% for A3, and 24.25% for A4. A3 had the highest observed correctness and significantly exceeded A1, A2, and A4 in the pre-specified paired correctness analysis, while A1 retained the highest policy-correct rate and the lowest unsafe-or-invalid rate. A4 had the lowest mean API cost and lowest false-refusal rate. On a preselected 150-case stability subset, answer-correct repeatability ranged from 92.00% to 98.67%. The results support a trade-off interpretation rather than a universal ranking: additional structural constraints changed failure modes and efficiency, but did not monotonically improve correctness or solve ambiguity and multi-turn state consistency.

AI.tldr: SemPlan Benchmark compares four architectures for natural-language interfaces to enterprise data, showing A3 (structured semantic-request generation with deterministic planning) performs best on correctness, but overall performance is low (22-26%) with trade-offs between different metrics.
AI.motivation: Natural-language interfaces to enterprise data need to handle underspecified requests while controlling invalid queries, policy failures, cost, and nondeterminism. There's a need to evaluate different architectural approaches for translating natural language into governed, executable behavior.
AI.method: Uses SemPlan Benchmark with 1,800 bilingual cases (English and Brazilian Portuguese). Compares four architectures under same model configuration: A1 (direct SQL generation), A2 (bounded tool-agent baseline), A3 (structured semantic-request generation + deterministic planning/execution), and A4 (clarification/stateful semantic-plan variant). Evaluates on 1,200-case frozen scientific subset.
AI.result: Overall correctness was low (22.25-25.67%). A3 had highest correctness (25.67%) and significantly exceeded other architectures in paired analysis. A1 had highest policy-correct rate and lowest unsafe/invalid rate. A4 had lowest mean API cost and lowest false-refusal rate. Stability repeatability ranged 92-98.67%.
AI.conclusion: Results support trade-off interpretation rather than universal ranking. Additional structural constraints changed failure modes and efficiency but didn't monotonically improve correctness or solve ambiguity and multi-turn state consistency challenges.

title: CutClean: Neural Network Pruning for Privacy-Preserving Inference
summary: Neural networks are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications with growing privacy leakage concerns. We show that this privacy leakage can occur even in the absence of representation imbalances that lead to traditional dataset biases. This poses significant privacy risks when deploying models that process sensitive attributes. In this context, we propose CutClean, a privacy-aware pruning method that allows to reduce privacy information flow through the network, while increasing its sparsity. Our approach employs auxiliary linear privacy heads placed at each network's block to quantify information leakage, and further applies increasing levels of sparsity to remove the private attribute leakage, measured in terms of the accuracy of the privacy head attached to the last block. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach effectively minimizes private information flow while achieving high sparsity rates and preserving classification target accuracy.

AI.tldr: CutClean is a privacy-aware pruning method that reduces privacy information leakage in neural networks while increasing sparsity, using auxiliary linear privacy heads to measure and remove private attribute leakage.
AI.motivation: Neural networks are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications with growing privacy leakage concerns, which can occur even without traditional dataset biases, posing significant privacy risks when processing sensitive attributes.
AI.method: CutClean uses auxiliary linear privacy heads placed at each network block to quantify information leakage, and applies increasing levels of sparsity to remove private attribute leakage measured by the accuracy of the privacy head attached to the last block.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the approach effectively minimizes private information flow while achieving high sparsity rates and preserving classification target accuracy.
AI.conclusion: CutClean provides an effective privacy-aware pruning method that addresses privacy leakage in neural networks without compromising sparsity or target task accuracy.

title: How Compliant is Sepsis Treatment? An Expert-Guided Neuro-symbolic Pipeline for Generating Clinical Compliance Insights
comment: This has been submitted and accepted in NeSy 2026 (https://2026.nesyconf.org/)
summary: Verifying whether clinical care follows evidence-based protocols is a natural neuro-symbolic problem, yet the safety-critical setting defeats either paradigm alone. We present an expert-guided pipeline that constrains a large language model strictly to semantic normalization, mapping messy drug and microbiology strings onto a fixed clinical vocabulary, while a Sugeno fuzzy inference system reasons over the normalized events. The fuzzy layer encodes eight Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundle rules and replaces binary judgments with graded scores in [0,1]. Applied to 2,438 MIMIC-IV v3.1 sepsis episodes, it surfaces antibiotic timing as the most critical breakdown (mean 0.24, 13% within one hour), Hour-1 underperformance (mean 36.7%), a 51% elevated-lactate drop-off, and descriptive differences in ICU stay across compliance groups (3.8 versus 5.1 days).

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic pipeline combining an LLM for semantic normalization of clinical data and a fuzzy inference system for graded assessment of sepsis care compliance, revealing key protocol breakdowns in antibiotic timing and other metrics.
AI.motivation: Clinical care verification against evidence-based protocols is a safety-critical problem that neither pure neural nor pure symbolic approaches alone can solve effectively in medical settings.
AI.method: Expert-guided pipeline with an LLM constrained to semantic normalization (mapping messy drug/microbiology strings to fixed vocabulary), coupled with a Sugeno fuzzy inference system encoding eight Surviving Sepsis Campaign rules to produce graded compliance scores (0-1).
AI.result: Applied to 2,438 MIMIC-IV v3.1 sepsis episodes, the system identified: antibiotic timing as the most critical breakdown (mean score 0.24, only 13% within one hour), Hour-1 underperformance (mean 36.7%), 51% elevated-lactate drop-off, and ICU stay differences (3.8 vs 5.1 days) across compliance groups.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach combining LLMs for data normalization and fuzzy logic for graded reasoning effectively identifies critical breakdowns in sepsis care compliance, providing nuanced assessment beyond binary judgments.

title: PPAPlace: Differentiable Cross-Stage Objectives for Chip Placement Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables, accepted at ICCAD 2026
summary: Macro placement significantly affects a chip's post-route performance, power, and area (PPA). Most placement methods optimize half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) as the primary objective. However, recent benchmarking shows a near-zero correlation between HPWL and post-route timing metrics such as the worst negative slack (WNS) and total negative slack (TNS). As a result, all six evaluated artificial intelligence (AI) placers degraded PPA relative to the hierarchical baseline. Recent efforts have tried to train cross-stage predictors to close this gap. However, existing methods focus on macro-only representations and use pre-route metrics as training labels. A label fidelity study of ten circuits at four design flow stages reveals that HPWL and pre-route timing poorly reflect final post-route timing rankings. In contrast, post-global-routing achieves the best balance between final timing fidelity and label generation cost-effectiveness. Based on this finding, PPAPlace is a timing-driven differentiable surrogate predicting post-route PPA from macro and standard-cell placements. The surrogate is a dual-stream predictor that combines graph attention over the chip netlist with spatial convolution over the placement grid. It is trained on post-global-routing labels. The predicted WNS and TNS gradients flow end-to-end back to cell coordinates. PPAPlace exploits these gradients in two ways: as a co-objective injected into an analytical placer's optimization loop (PPAPlace-CoOpt), and as a post-placement refinement step that adjusts macro positions via projected gradient descent (PPAPlace-Refine). On five ChiPBench test circuits excluded from training, PPAPlace improves average WNS and TNS by 22\% and 51\% over the hierarchical baseline while preserving power and routability, using the same predictor without test-circuit retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/ValleyC/PPAPlace.

AI.tldr: PPAPlace is a timing-driven differentiable surrogate model that predicts post-route PPA from macro and standard-cell placements, using post-global-routing labels to address the poor correlation between traditional HPWL metrics and actual post-route timing.
AI.motivation: Traditional placement methods optimize half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL), but recent benchmarking shows near-zero correlation between HPWL and actual post-route timing metrics (WNS/TNS), causing AI placers to degrade PPA relative to baselines. Existing methods use macro-only representations and pre-route metrics that poorly reflect final timing rankings.
AI.method: Developed PPAPlace: a dual-stream differentiable surrogate combining graph attention over chip netlist with spatial convolution over placement grid. Trained on post-global-routing labels for better fidelity-cost balance. Two applications: 1) PPAPlace-CoOpt injects predicted timing gradients into analytical placer optimization loop; 2) PPAPlace-Refine adjusts macro positions via projected gradient descent as post-placement refinement.
AI.result: On five ChiPBench test circuits excluded from training, PPAPlace improves average worst negative slack (WNS) by 22% and total negative slack (TNS) by 51% over hierarchical baseline while preserving power and routability, without test-circuit retraining.
AI.conclusion: Post-global-routing provides the best balance for timing prediction fidelity versus cost. The PPAPlace framework successfully bridges the gap between placement optimization and post-route PPA by using timing-driven differentiable surrogates trained on appropriate intermediate-stage labels.

title: Algorithm Design and Physician Liability
comment: 65 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables; includes online appendix (pp. 51-65)
summary: A single clinical algorithm can deliver unequal accuracy across patient groups, and concern about such disparity has grown as artificial intelligence (AI) spreads through clinical decision-making. In response, a liability rule introduced in the United States holds healthcare providers responsible when their reliance on disparate algorithms contributes to erroneous clinical decisions. We examine how such liability considerations reshape (i) an AI firm's algorithm design decisions that drive group-specific accuracy and (ii) a physician's decisions to use AI in healthcare delivery. The AI firm designs an algorithm for two patient groups, and improving accuracy for the disadvantaged group is more costly. The physician (who remains the accountable decision-maker) then decides whether to consult AI, weighing the reduction in clinical uncertainty against expected liability exposure when AI errors disproportionately affect the disadvantaged group. We find the liability rule can induce disparate use of AI: the physician may reduce AI use overall and, over an intermediate range of liability, rely on AI less for disadvantaged patients. The effect is non-monotone. As liability increases, the physician's use of AI for disadvantaged patients first declines, then rises as the firm reallocates investment toward reducing disparity or switches to an equal-accuracy design. Mandating equal algorithmic accuracy across patient groups can then inadvertently harm both groups, because a uniform accuracy requirement distorts the firm's investment incentives and the physician's equilibrium AI-use decisions.

AI.tldr: A liability rule for disparate AI algorithms in healthcare can lead to non-monotonic, disparate AI usage patterns, where physicians may reduce AI use for disadvantaged patients, and equal-accuracy mandates can harm both patient groups.
AI.motivation: Concern about algorithmic disparity in clinical AI is growing as AI spreads through healthcare. A U.S. liability rule holds providers responsible when reliance on disparate algorithms contributes to erroneous decisions, creating tensions between algorithmic design, clinical use, and liability exposure.
AI.method: The paper uses an economic modeling approach with two main actors: (1) an AI firm that designs algorithms for two patient groups with different cost structures (more costly to improve accuracy for disadvantaged group), and (2) a physician who decides whether to use AI, weighing clinical uncertainty reduction against expected liability exposure from AI errors that disproportionately affect disadvantaged patients.
AI.result: The liability rule induces disparate AI use: physicians may reduce overall AI use and, over an intermediate liability range, rely less on AI for disadvantaged patients. The effect is non-monotonic - as liability increases, AI use for disadvantaged patients first declines, then rises as firms reallocate investment or switch to equal-accuracy designs. Equal-accuracy mandates can harm both patient groups by distorting investment incentives and equilibrium AI-use decisions.
AI.conclusion: Healthcare AI liability rules create complex, non-monotonic effects on algorithmic design and clinical usage patterns. Simple regulatory solutions like mandating equal algorithmic accuracy across groups can have unintended negative consequences for both patient groups by distorting economic incentives in the AI-physician decision-making system.

title: Recent Advances in Deep Learning-Based Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
summary: Computational approaches to drug discovery involve multiple sub-problems, and among them, drug-target binding affinity prediction plays an important role. Despite recent advances, accurately predicting binding affinity remains an open research area. The major objective of our paper is to perform a comprehensive review and comparative analysis of recent machine learning methods for drug-target binding affinity prediction, with a focus on identifying strengths, limitations, and research gaps. We review representative recent deep learning approaches that use common benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, covering a range of neural network architectures and representation strategies. In addition, we analyze seven widely used benchmark datasets and commonly adopted evaluation metrics for drug-target binding affinity prediction. Our analysis indicates that although many methods report strong performance on standard benchmarks, their effectiveness is often influenced by dataset bias and limited evaluation settings. Furthermore, most methods exhibit reduced performance in cold-start scenarios, highlighting challenges in generalization. We identify several limitations of current approaches, including dataset imbalance, the lack of standardized evaluation, limited real-world applicability, and challenges in cold-start scenarios. We also discuss future research directions, including better dataset design, more robust evaluation methods, improved handling of cold-start problems, and the integration of multimodal representations.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive review paper analyzing recent machine learning methods for drug-target binding affinity prediction, covering architectures, datasets, evaluation metrics, and identifying limitations like dataset bias and cold-start challenges.
AI.motivation: Drug-target binding affinity prediction is crucial for computational drug discovery but remains an open research problem with accuracy challenges. The paper aims to provide a comprehensive review and comparative analysis of recent ML methods to identify strengths, limitations, and research gaps in this important field.
AI.method: The paper conducts a systematic review and comparative analysis of recent deep learning approaches for binding affinity prediction. It examines representative methods using common benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, covering various neural network architectures and representation strategies. The analysis includes seven widely used benchmark datasets and commonly adopted evaluation metrics.
AI.result: While many methods report strong performance on standard benchmarks, their effectiveness is often influenced by dataset bias and limited evaluation settings. Most methods show reduced performance in cold-start scenarios, indicating generalization challenges. Key limitations identified include dataset imbalance, lack of standardized evaluation, limited real-world applicability, and cold-start problems.
AI.conclusion: Current approaches for drug-target binding affinity prediction face significant challenges despite reported benchmark performance. The review identifies critical gaps and proposes future research directions including better dataset design, more robust evaluation methods, improved cold-start problem handling, and integration of multimodal representations.

title: Your Probabilistic JEPA Is Secretly a Hidden Markov Model: A State-Space Interpretation of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning
comment: 69 pages
summary: A hidden Markov model (HMM) combines three roles: inference of a hidden-state belief from observations, propagation through a Markov transition, and emission back to observation space. We show that full, time-indexed Predictive Information Bottleneck VJEPA (PIB-VJEPA) exposes the same computational structure: a stochastic context encoder plays the role of an amortized filtering distribution, a probabilistic predictor defines latent-state dynamics, and a decoder, inverse target encoder, or induced implicit conditional supplies the emission direction. We distinguish 4 progressively stronger levels of correspondence and give sufficient conditions for exact sequence-level HMM equivalence. To make the connection concrete, we introduce Markov-Chain JEPA (MCJEPA), which replaces the latent predictor by a learned transition matrix; in the finite time-homogeneous case, matrix powers guarantee exact multi-horizon Chapman--Kolmogorov consistency. Conditioned discrete-state transitions, continuous-state Markov kernels, and continuous-time dynamics extend this construction, while deterministic temporal JEPA appears as a degenerate Dirac-kernel special case. We further interpret predictive information-bottleneck learning as seeking a compact predictive state: compression promotes minimality, while residual predictability tests sufficiency. Controlled experiments support transition composition, the filtering interpretation, predictive Markovization in a known synthetic process, and the distinction between JEPA latent prediction and HMM-style sequence learning. Together, these results give temporal JEPA a principled state-space interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that predictive information bottleneck VJEPA (PIB-VJEPA) shares the same computational structure as hidden Markov models (HMMs), with stochastic context encoder as filtering distribution, predictor as latent dynamics, and decoder as emission. It introduces Markov-Chain JEPA (MCJEPA) for exact HMM equivalence and interprets predictive learning as seeking compact predictive states.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to establish a principled state-space interpretation for temporal JEPA models by connecting them to the well-established theoretical framework of hidden Markov models. The authors aim to show that VJEPA's computational structure naturally corresponds to HMM components, providing theoretical grounding for predictive learning approaches.
AI.method: The method involves: 1) Analyzing correspondence between VJEPA components (context encoder, predictor, decoder) and HMM roles (filtering, transition, emission), 2) Introducing Markov-Chain JEPA (MCJEPA) with learned transition matrix for exact HMM equivalence, 3) Demonstrating conditions for Chapman-Kolmogorov consistency in finite time-homogeneous case, 4) Extending to discrete/continuous state spaces and continuous-time dynamics, 5) Conducting controlled experiments to validate the theoretical connections.
AI.result: Results show: 1) Four progressively stronger levels of correspondence between VJEPA and HMMs, 2) Sufficient conditions for exact sequence-level HMM equivalence, 3) MCJEPA enables exact multi-horizon consistency via matrix powers, 4) Predictive information bottleneck learning seeks compact predictive states (compression promotes minimality, predictability tests sufficiency), 5) Experiments support transition composition, filtering interpretation, and predictive Markovization in synthetic processes.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully gives temporal JEPA a principled state-space interpretation by establishing formal connections to hidden Markov models. The theoretical framework shows VJEPA naturally implements HMM-like computation, with MCJEPA providing exact equivalence. This bridges predictive learning approaches with classical state-space models, offering theoretical grounding for VJEPA's architecture and learning objectives.

title: Dynamic Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing with Online Requests: Event-Driven Transformer--DRL and Rolling-Horizon Benchmarking
comment: 7 Pages
summary: This paper presents an event-driven learning and benchmarking framework for the Dynamic Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing Problem with progressively revealed requests and evolving vehicle states. Masked MLP and Transformer policies are trained through behavior cloning and proximal policy optimization. Deterministic feasibility masking prevents invalid vehicle--request assignments, while fixed-prefix/flexible-suffix route commitments protect completed, active, and near-term decisions and separately measure vehicle reassignment and resequencing. The learned policies are compared with dynamic insertion heuristics and time-limited rolling-horizon optimization. In a 20-scenario policy benchmark, all methods completed every request without invalid actions, but nearest feasible achieved the lowest mean objective and outperformed the learned policies in routing quality, waiting time, stability, makespan, and runtime. Across five independent training runs, PPO had little average effect on the MLP and improved the Transformer on average, although with greater seed variability. Under the common protocol, nearest feasible achieved the lowest combined objective and route disruption, whereas rolling horizon achieved the lowest waiting times and makespan at substantially higher computational cost. The learned policies retained millisecond-level decisions and transferred to instances with up to 80 requests without retraining, but did not outperform the strongest heuristic. No single method was best across routing efficiency, service responsiveness, stability, and online computation.

AI.tldr: A framework for dynamic multi-depot vehicle routing with progressive request reveals and evolving vehicle states, comparing masked MLP/Transformer policies (trained via behavior cloning/PPO) against dynamic insertion heuristics and rolling-horizon optimization.
AI.motivation: Address the dynamic multi-depot vehicle routing problem where requests are revealed progressively over time and vehicle states evolve, requiring online decision-making that balances routing efficiency, service responsiveness, solution stability, and computational cost.
AI.method: Develop event-driven learning framework using masked MLP and Transformer policies trained through behavior cloning and proximal policy optimization. Use deterministic feasibility masking to prevent invalid assignments and fixed-prefix/flexible-suffix route commitments to protect completed/active decisions while measuring vehicle reassignment/resequencing.
AI.result: In 20-scenario benchmark: all methods completed all requests without invalid actions. Nearest feasible heuristic achieved lowest mean objective and outperformed learned policies on routing quality, waiting time, stability, makespan, and runtime. PPO had minimal average effect on MLP but improved Transformer with greater seed variability. Learned policies had millisecond decisions and transferred to instances with up to 80 requests without retraining.
AI.conclusion: While learned policies enabled fast online decisions and good transferability, they didn't outperform strongest heuristics. No single method dominated across all metrics (routing efficiency, service responsiveness, stability, online computation), highlighting trade-offs in dynamic routing problem design.

title: ARC: Fair Relative Advantage Comparison in Open-Ended Real-World Interaction
summary: Open-ended real-world interaction admits multiple valid behaviors: an agent may answer directly, ask for clarification, provide progress updates, or confirm before acting. This flexibility breaks a core assumption behind group-based RL: rollouts compared within a group are no longer guaranteed to be behaviorally comparable. As a result, reward-model preferences over interaction style can distort relative advantages and steer optimization toward reward-preferred behaviors rather than context-appropriate ones. We formalize this as a \textit{reward fairness problem} and propose \textbf{ARC} (Advantage Regularization via Conditioning), a training recipe that restores fairer relative comparison through strategy-conditioned rollout grouping, together with hybrid rewards and entropy regularization. We study ARC in our proposed \inter, a novel paradigm for responsive, steerable, and execution-aware user-agent interaction that decouples user-visible communication from latent reasoning and tool use. \inter\ also provides the annotation and distillation pipeline for constructing \inter-86K, our strategy-annotated training corpus for supervised and RL training. Empirically, ARC substantially strengthens the core $τ/τ^2$ tool-use benchmarks, while \inter\ reduces time-to-first-token from 4.91s to 1.27s relative to a think-style baseline. Together, these results suggest that a central bottleneck in open-ended interactive learning is not only how agents are rewarded, but whether their behaviors are compared fairly in the first place. The ARC implementation and \inter-86K training data will be released.

AI.tldr: ARC (Advantage Regularization via Conditioning) addresses reward fairness problems in open-ended real-world interactions by using strategy-conditioned rollout grouping, hybrid rewards, and entropy regularization to ensure fair behavioral comparisons during RL training.
AI.motivation: Open-ended real-world interactions break core RL assumptions because multiple valid behaviors exist for any given situation. Traditional group-based RL fails when rollouts within a group aren't behaviorally comparable, causing reward-model preferences to distort relative advantages and steer optimization toward reward-preferred rather than context-appropriate behaviors.
AI.method: Proposes ARC training recipe featuring: 1) Strategy-conditioned rollout grouping for fairer relative comparisons, 2) Hybrid rewards, and 3) Entropy regularization. Also introduces \inter paradigm for responsive, steerable user-agent interaction that decouples visible communication from latent reasoning/tool use, plus annotation/distillation pipeline for INTER-86K strategy-annotated training corpus.
AI.result: ARC substantially strengthens core τ/τ² tool-use benchmarks, while \inter reduces time-to-first-token from 4.91s to 1.27s relative to a think-style baseline. Demonstrates that fair behavioral comparison is a central bottleneck in open-ended interactive learning.
AI.conclusion: The key bottleneck in open-ended interactive learning is not just how agents are rewarded, but whether their behaviors are compared fairly. ARC provides an effective solution to reward fairness problems, and \inter enables more responsive, steerable interactions while dramatically improving response latency.

title: Stochastic Control Policies for Robust Molecular Transition Path Sampling
summary: Transition path sampling (TPS) aims to efficiently generate rare molecular transition trajectories between metastable states and is essential for understanding biomolecular mechanisms. Beyond traditional molecular dynamics (MD)-based sampling, machine learning has become central to state-of-the-art TPS. One major class of methods learns control forces during explicit MD rollouts. By preserving the underlying molecular dynamics, these methods tend to produce more physically plausible trajectories than endpoint-conditioned generators that construct paths directly. However, rollout-based control methods have been reported to exhibit unstable and strongly seed-dependent performance. We recast rollout-based control as learning a path-space proposal distribution and investigate stochasticity placement as a design choice for improving exploration and optimization robustness. We develop two stochastic policies: FS-TPS, which directly parameterizes a state-dependent Gaussian distribution over the control policy output, and LaS-TPS, which samples a compact latent control variable and decodes it into structured, cross-atom-correlated force variation. We conduct extensive multi-seed experiments on three biomolecular systems of increasing size: alanine dipeptide, chignolin, and BBL, a fast-folding protein. Stochastic policies consistently improve transition success and path quality over deterministic-policy baselines while substantially reducing sensitivity to random initialization.

AI.tldr: Stochastic policies in rollout-based transition path sampling improve exploration and robustness over deterministic methods.
AI.motivation: Machine learning-based TPS methods using rollout-based control have unstable and seed-dependent performance. The paper investigates stochasticity placement to improve exploration and optimization robustness in TPS.
AI.method: Developed two stochastic policies: FS-TPS (parameterizes state-dependent Gaussian distribution over control policy output) and LaS-TPS (samples compact latent control variable that decodes into structured, cross-atom-correlated force variation).
AI.result: Extensive multi-seed experiments on three biomolecular systems (alanine dipeptide, chignolin, BBL protein) show stochastic policies consistently improve transition success and path quality over deterministic baselines while reducing sensitivity to random initialization.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic policies address the instability issues of rollout-based control methods in TPS, offering more robust and exploration-enhanced path sampling for biomolecular systems.

title: Reward Machines for Signal Temporal Logic
summary: Signal temporal logic (STL) provides a formal language for specifying real-time properties of real-valued observations, along with a quantitative robustness score for monitoring satisfaction. Control synthesis from STL specifications is of interest since manual controller design becomes infeasible as real-world systems grow in complexity. Moreover, many modern autonomous and AI-enabled systems lack accurate and complete system models, which makes optimization-based synthesis approaches unsuitable and motivates learning-based control. Prior work uses STL robustness scores as rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) to obtain control policies satisfying given specifications; however, robustness depends on execution history, leading to intractable state space expansion for general long-horizon specifications with arbitrarily nested temporal operators. This work introduces a novel automata-based approach that provides an efficient memory mechanism and associated Markovian rewards suitable for RL frameworks. Our approach constructs a timed alternating automaton from the given STL specifications, augments the state space with automaton locations and clock valuations, and derives rewards from the automaton acceptance condition. We empirically demonstrate that our approach learns policies that achieve higher robustness scores and satisfaction rates than those learned by existing approaches using robustness-based rewards.

AI.tldr: STL-constrained RL with automata-based memory mechanism for efficient learning of control policies from temporal logic specifications
AI.motivation: Control synthesis from STL specifications is needed as manual controller design becomes infeasible for complex systems. Many modern systems lack accurate models, making optimization-based approaches unsuitable and motivating learning-based control. Existing RL approaches using STL robustness scores suffer from state space explosion for long-horizon specifications with nested temporal operators due to non-Markovian nature of robustness.
AI.method: Introduces an automata-based approach that constructs a timed alternating automaton from STL specifications, augments the state space with automaton locations and clock valuations, and derives Markovian rewards from the automaton acceptance condition. This provides an efficient memory mechanism suitable for RL frameworks.
AI.result: Empirical demonstration shows that the approach learns policies achieving higher robustness scores and satisfaction rates than existing approaches using robustness-based rewards.
AI.conclusion: The automata-based approach effectively addresses the state space explosion problem in RL for STL-constrained control by providing efficient memory mechanisms and Markovian rewards, leading to better learning performance for complex temporal specifications.

title: HI-MeshGraphNets: Efficient and Accurate Mesh-based Physics Learning with Hierarchical Multi-scale Graph Neural Networks
summary:
Machine-learned physical surrogate models have become promising alternatives to mesh-based numerical solvers. Among them, graph neural networks (GNNs) are well suited for representing simulation meshes and learning nodal state evolution through message passing. However, conventional flat message passing becomes inefficient on large, high-fidelity meshes because information propagates only one hop per layer, requiring deep processors for long-range interactions and increasing computational cost, memory usage, and the risk of over-smoothing.
  To address this limitation, we propose Hierarchical Interpolating MeshGraphNets (HI-MGN), a multiscale extension of MeshGraphNets for efficient long-range communication on unstructured meshes. HI-MGN replaces the flat processor with a hierarchical multiscale processor that coarsens graphs using farthest-point sampling and Voronoi partitioning while preserving the original mesh topology. Message passing on coarse graphs enables information to travel over larger geometric distances with fewer layers, and a learned graph interpolation network reconstructs fine-resolution features.
  Across three structural and fluid benchmarks, HI-MGN achieves improved accuracy compared with MeshGraphNets and the Bi-Stride Multi-Scale GNN while reducing training time and peak memory usage. The results show that topology-aware hierarchical message passing and learned coarse-to-fine interpolation provide an effective and practical framework for scalable mesh-based physics surrogate modeling.

AI.tldr: HI-MGN: A multiscale graph neural network for physics simulation that uses hierarchical message passing on coarsened meshes to improve efficiency and accuracy compared to flat approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional flat message passing in GNN-based physics surrogates is inefficient for large, high-fidelity meshes because information propagates only one hop per layer, requiring deep processors for long-range interactions, which increases computational cost, memory usage, and risk of over-smoothing.
AI.method: HI-MGN replaces the flat processor with a hierarchical multiscale processor that coarsens graphs using farthest-point sampling and Voronoi partitioning while preserving original mesh topology. Message passing on coarse graphs enables information to travel larger distances with fewer layers, and a learned graph interpolation network reconstructs fine-resolution features.
AI.result: HI-MGN achieves improved accuracy compared with MeshGraphNets and Bi-Stride Multi-Scale GNN across three structural and fluid benchmarks while reducing training time and peak memory usage.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware hierarchical message passing and learned coarse-to-fine interpolation provide an effective and practical framework for scalable mesh-based physics surrogate modeling.

title: A Calibrated Test of Internal Action Maps: State Signals Without Global Affine Closure
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; includes supplementary results and ancillary reproducibility files
summary: A hidden state signal can be decodable or causally usable without supporting a reusable action map. We test whether action maps fitted without a source reach its natural post-action activation and compose. We organize the tests as an evidence lattice and validate the geometric branch on a known affine S_5 carrier: all held-source folds pass one-step, composition, inverse, decoding, and commutativity gates. Structured curvature and held-domain conjugacy raise error monotonically, but only 23/30 strongest cells flip a closure gate, bounding rather than universalizing calibration. In post-trained Qwen/Qwen3-4B, frozen final-token h28 affine maps have mean held-entity error .519, versus .398 for within-test-domain cross-fit. Seven randomized entity splits and map geometry do not support a purely entity-specific account. Earlier h4/h16 layers fit one-step transitions better, but h4 conflict-state decoding is weak and lexical controls remain unresolved. Three matched intervention datasets regenerated from one frozen checkpoint show causal effects only at h28/h36. Outcome-aware refitting improves h28 one-step error to .474 (.469 with weighting), yet no refit passes composition. Learned finite worlds likewise preserve relative algebraic signals or shared charts without held-source affine closure. Within the tested carriers, state availability, causal use, local geometry, and reusable closure are separable. The result is limited to one pretrained model, sampled final-token layers, two finite worlds, and the tested affine or diagnostic function classes.

AI.tldr: Action maps can be decodable and causally usable without supporting reusable composition, with geometry and causal closure separable within tested affine carriers.
AI.motivation: To test whether action maps fitted without source information can reach natural post-action activation and composition, examining the relationship between state availability, causal use, local geometry, and reusable closure.
AI.method: Organized tests as an evidence lattice, validated on known affine S_5 carrier. Tested composition, inverse, decoding, and commutativity gates. Used post-trained Qwen/Qwen3-4B model with frozen final-token affine maps, analyzed earlier layers, conducted randomized entity splits, and performed matched intervention datasets from frozen checkpoints.
AI.result: Action maps show mean held-entity error .519 vs .398 for within-test-domain cross-fit. Earlier layers fit one-step transitions better but have weak conflict-state decoding. Causal effects only appear at h28/h36 layers. Refitting improves one-step error but never passes composition. Structured curvature and held-domain conjugacy raise error monotonically but not universally.
AI.conclusion: Within tested carriers, state availability, causal use, local geometry, and reusable closure are separable - a hidden state signal can be decodable or causally usable without supporting a reusable action map. Limitations: single pretrained model, sampled layers, two finite worlds, tested affine/diagnostic classes.

title: Federated Prompt Learning: A Unified Framework, Empirical Analysis, and Future Directions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become core components of cloud-based intelligent services in academia and industry, yet their training and deployment are hindered by high computational costs, data centralization, and privacy concerns. Federated learning (FL) offers a decentralized training paradigm that enables clients to collaboratively train a learning model without sharing raw data, making it a promising solution for privacy-preserving LLM training and reasoning. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of federated prompt learning (FPL) to review recent advances in integrating the federated learning paradigm and large language models, answering the following research questions: RQ1: The fundamental motivations, characteristics, and enabling technologies of FPL, and how it differs from conventional FL and full-model federated fine-tuning; RQ2: The trade-offs FPL approaches exhibit in performance, communication efficiency, computational overhead, scalability, personalization, and heterogeneity handling; RQ3: The remaining security, privacy, robustness, and system challenges, along with key future research directions. To this end, we systematically examine existing FPL methods across the full model lifecycle: pre-training, fine-tuning, and practical applications, while discussing security, privacy, and robustness issues and summarizing existing defense mechanisms. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future directions, aiming to help readers understand how the insights drive research in FPL.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey paper on Federated Prompt Learning (FPL), which integrates federated learning with large language models to address computational costs, data centralization, and privacy concerns in LLM deployment.
AI.motivation: LLMs face challenges with high computational costs, data centralization, and privacy concerns. Federated learning offers a decentralized approach that allows collaborative training without sharing raw data, making it promising for privacy-preserving LLM training and reasoning.
AI.method: The paper is a survey that systematically examines existing FPL methods across the full model lifecycle: pre-training, fine-tuning, and practical applications. It reviews recent advances and answers three key research questions about FPL fundamentals, trade-offs, and remaining challenges.
AI.result: The survey provides a comprehensive review of FPL approaches, examining their performance, communication efficiency, computational overhead, scalability, personalization, and heterogeneity handling trade-offs. It also discusses security, privacy, robustness issues and existing defense mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: FPL represents a promising approach for privacy-preserving LLM training. The paper highlights open challenges and future research directions to help advance the field and drive further research in federated prompt learning.

title: Exploring ESC Winners with Nested Diagrams
comment: Accepted for CONCEPTS 2026 Data Analysis Showcase (CDAS)
summary:
We present ConceptFlow, a scikit-learn-compatible Python library for Formal Concept Analysis that constructs and renders nested line diagrams from many-valued formal contexts. Given a many-valued context and a partition of its attributes into conceptual scales, ConceptFlow performs conceptual scaling, computes the factor lattices, identifies filled nodes of the corresponding subdirect product, and produces an interactive visualization.
  We apply ConceptFlow to the winners of the Eurovision Song Contest from 1975 to 2025, exploring relationships between voting patterns and musical characteristics. Voting support is captured by an outer scale spanning regional, cultural, historical, and political dimensions, while an inner scale captures musical characteristics via tempo and key. The resulting nested line diagram reveals implications across both scales, exposing dependencies between how winning entries were voted for and the musical properties they share.

AI.tldr: ConceptFlow is a Python library for Formal Concept Analysis that visualizes many-valued contexts as nested line diagrams. It was used to analyze Eurovision Song Contest winners (1975-2025) to reveal relationships between voting patterns and musical characteristics.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to provide a scikit-learn-compatible tool for Formal Concept Analysis that can handle many-valued contexts and produce interactive visualizations. The Eurovision analysis demonstrates practical application for exploring complex relationships between voting patterns and musical properties.
AI.method: ConceptFlow performs conceptual scaling on many-valued contexts partitioned into conceptual scales, computes factor lattices, identifies filled nodes in subdirect products, and produces interactive nested line diagram visualizations. For Eurovision, voting support uses an outer scale (regional, cultural, historical, political dimensions) and musical characteristics use an inner scale (tempo, key).
AI.result: The library successfully constructs and renders nested line diagrams. The Eurovision application reveals implications across both scales, exposing dependencies between how winning entries were voted for and the musical properties they share, providing insights into relationships between voting patterns and musical characteristics.
AI.conclusion: ConceptFlow is an effective tool for Formal Concept Analysis that enables interactive exploration of complex datasets through nested line diagrams. The Eurovision case study demonstrates its utility in uncovering meaningful relationships in multidimensional data, particularly between voting behavior and musical attributes.

title: Geometric Filtering of LLM-Generated Samples for Few-Shot Text Classification
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, to be published in IEEE LACCI 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate synthetic training data for text classification, but the quality of generated samples is heterogeneous: some fall in correct class regions of the embedding space while others land in peripheral or cross-class zones. We propose a geometric filtering framework that evaluates each LLM-generated sample by its Euclidean distance to real class examples in a sentence embedding space, selecting only geometrically consistent candidates. A soft weighting mechanism transforms filter scores into sample weights for classifier training. Evaluated across 13 datasets, 5 classifiers, 10 augmentation methods, and over 6,700 configurations, our method achieves +2.61 percentage points (pp) over SMOTE ($p<0.0001$, Cohen's $d=0.95$, 88.9% win rate). The approach generalizes to named entity recognition (+9.26pp, 100% win rate) without filter modification, and is robust across 5 LLMs from 4 providers. A key finding is that the simplest distance-based filter consistently outperforms complex multi-criteria alternatives.

AI.tldr: A geometric filtering framework that selects high-quality LLM-generated samples based on Euclidean distance to real examples in embedding space, improving text classification and NER performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate synthetic training data for text classification, but sample quality is heterogeneous - some samples are in correct class regions while others are in peripheral or cross-class zones, requiring effective filtering methods.
AI.method: Proposes a geometric filtering framework that evaluates LLM-generated samples by Euclidean distance to real class examples in sentence embedding space, selecting only geometrically consistent candidates. Uses soft weighting mechanism to transform filter scores into sample weights for classifier training.
AI.result: Across 13 datasets, 5 classifiers, 10 augmentation methods, and over 6,700 configurations: achieves +2.61 percentage points over SMOTE (p<0.0001, Cohen's d=0.95, 88.9% win rate). Generalizes to named entity recognition (+9.26pp, 100% win rate) without filter modification, robust across 5 LLMs from 4 providers. Key finding: simplest distance-based filter consistently outperforms complex multi-criteria alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Geometric filtering based on Euclidean distance in embedding space is an effective, simple, and robust approach for selecting high-quality LLM-generated synthetic training data, outperforming existing methods and generalizing across tasks and models.

title: Ontology-Grounded Project Memory for Coding Agents
comment: 5 pages. Accepted at NeSy 2026 (Industry Track); to appear in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research vol. 284. Benchmark artifact: https://github.com/Trivyn/moosedev
summary: Coding agents have become the primary means of generating new code in many software projects, and the resulting velocity of changes makes keeping track of the reasons behind those changes challenging. This paper introduces MOOSEDev, a system designed to give coding agents structured, ontology-grounded project memory. The system captures architectural decisions, lessons, constraints, and rationales in a knowledge graph exposed to agents via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Records carry lifecycle status, provenance, and supersession links, queryable via MOOSE, a proprietary neurosymbolic engine that treats the symbolic layer as the primary reasoning substrate. We compared MOOSEDev against a production vector-memory tool on a neutral public corpus of 835 typed records. MOOSEDev returned the expected answer set essentially in full (0.98-1.00) on supersession, set-completeness, and negation questions, whereas the baseline's top-k retrieval surfaced between 6% and 27%. Conversely, relevance recall and token cost were largely equivalent between the two systems. We also describe a temporal commit-history bootstrap of our own codebase, a pre-registered live trial, and lessons learned.

AI.tldr: MOOSEDev is a system that gives coding agents structured, ontology-grounded project memory using a knowledge graph with lifecycle status, provenance, and supersession links, outperforming vector-memory tools on certain queries while maintaining similar relevance recall.
AI.motivation: Coding agents generate code at high velocity, making it challenging to track the reasons behind code changes and maintain project memory of architectural decisions, lessons, constraints, and rationales.
AI.method: Developed MOOSEDev system that captures project knowledge in a structured, ontology-grounded knowledge graph exposed to agents via Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Uses MOOSE, a proprietary neurosymbolic engine with symbolic layer as primary reasoning substrate. Records include lifecycle status, provenance, and supersession links.
AI.result: Tested on 835 typed records, MOOSEDev returned expected answer sets essentially in full (0.98-1.00) on supersession, set-completeness, and negation questions, while baseline vector-memory tool's top-k retrieval only surfaced 6-27%. Relevance recall and token costs were largely equivalent between systems.
AI.conclusion: MOOSEDev demonstrates that structured, ontology-grounded project memory with explicit modeling of record lifecycles and relationships significantly outperforms vector memory on certain complex query types while maintaining similar performance on relevance recall.

title: Variation Brownian Kernel Ladders
summary: Claims about the benefit of depth depend on the complexity assigned to a representation. We introduce the \emph{Variation Brownian Kernel Ladder} (VBKL), a path-atomic function-space framework that separates nonlinear recursive dictionary construction from linear variation superposition. Starting from linear projections, each atom recursively composes unit-ball profiles from the Brownian reproducing kernel Hilbert space; the full VBKL space is then the signed-measure variation hull of the completed dictionary. We identify each recursive dictionary as a union of Brownian pullback RKHS balls and establish variation-controlled Hölder regularity, compactness and attainment, and strict growth with depth under a local non-degeneracy condition whose trace lies in the support of the input measure. For associated finite lower-support architectures, we derive Rademacher and generalization bounds through Brownian quadratic chaos, signed threshold traces, and VC entropy. We also construct two-stage approximants by discretizing the outer measure and the selected outer Brownian profiles, obtaining an $M^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2}$ error bound, a sharp interpolation constant $\sqrt{A/2}$, and at most $2M$ active outer-profile basis contributions per evaluation. Controlled experiments illustrate the approximation mechanisms and indicate a favorable limited-data accuracy--complexity trade-off.

AI.tldr: VBKL introduces a depth-beneficial framework with recursive dictionary construction, showing improved approximation with depth under non-degeneracy conditions and establishing generalization bounds.
AI.motivation: Claims about depth benefits depend on representation complexity, motivating a framework to properly analyze depth advantages through recursive composition and variation superposition.
AI.method: Introduces Variation Brownian Kernel Ladder (VBKL): path-atomic function space with recursive dictionary construction from Brownian RKHS unit-ball profiles, then linear variation superposition to form signed-measure variation hull.
AI.result: Establishes variation-controlled Hölder regularity, compactness, strict depth growth under non-degeneracy; derives Rademacher/generalization bounds via Brownian quadratic chaos; obtains M⁻¹/²+m⁻¹/² approximation error with sharp interpolation constant.
AI.conclusion: VBKL demonstrates theoretical depth benefits with controlled generalization properties, showing favorable limited-data accuracy-complexity trade-off in experiments.

title: Second Thought: Reasoning in Parallel as LLM Agents Act and Observe
summary: LLM agents in the ReAct paradigm alternate between reasoning, acting, and observing, but deliberate reasoning is confined to the Thought phase: while the agent serializes an action and waits for the environment, its reasoning is frozen. We identify this recurring interval for Action and Observation as a reasoning idle window and ask whether it can host additional reasoning in parallel that serves future turns. Therefore, we propose Second Thought, a training-free inference framework that forks four auxiliary branches the instant each Thought phase concludes, decodes them concurrently with the main loop, and merges the generated thoughts back when the environment observation arrives. In this way, Second Thought relocates the added reasoning off the main thread's sequential decoding path. Across three agentic benchmarks and three reasoning LLMs, Second Thought lowers the average turn count in all nine (model,benchmark) pairs and reduces main thread decoding in six of them by up to 43% (roughly 20% on average among those settings), while leaving it essentially unchanged in a seventh; Pass@1 shows no significant change in seven of nine pairs and the two significant differences are +12.4 and +10.2 points. Against a compute-matched control that forces an equivalent budget onto the main thread's own reasoning, it attains strictly higher Pass@1 with 1.3 to 3.2 less sequential decoding in all four settings where the control applies.

AI.tldr: Second Thought enables concurrent reasoning during idle windows in LLM agent loops, improving efficiency without compromising performance.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents in the ReAct paradigm waste idle time during Action and Observation phases where reasoning is frozen, creating opportunities for parallel reasoning to serve future turns.
AI.method: A training-free inference framework that forks four auxiliary reasoning branches at the end of each Thought phase, decodes them concurrently with the main loop, and merges results when environment observation arrives, moving additional reasoning off the main thread.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks and three LLMs, Second Thought reduces average turn count in all nine pairs and main thread decoding by up to 43% (average ~20%) while maintaining Pass@1 performance. Outperforms compute-matched controls with higher Pass@1 and less sequential decoding.
AI.conclusion: Second Thought successfully leverages idle windows in agent loops for parallel reasoning, improving efficiency without sacrificing performance, representing a novel approach to optimizing LLM agent inference.

title: Fashion Outfit Generation via Unified Sequential Composition Models
summary: The task of synthesizing stylistically coherent fashion outfits from massive item libraries, known as fashion outfit generation, remains a non-trivial challenge, primarily due to the non-monotonic and implicit nature of aesthetic compatibility, coupled with the exponentially large combinatorial search space. In this paper, we formalize this task as Constrained Ensemble Generation (CEG) and model it as a finite-horizon deterministic Markov Decision Process. To address CEG in fashion, we propose the Unified Sequential Composition Model (USCM), which jointly models set-level compatibility and latent composition intents. Guided by USCM's learned priors, a Latent Expansion Monte Carlo Tree Search (LE-MCTS) mechanism is proposed to handle item retrieval during composition, balancing local aesthetic synergy with global structural balance. Extensive experiments on the Polyvore Outfits dataset, along with zero-shot evaluations on the iFashion and PolyvoreU datasets, demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance across independent human preference evaluations, automated aesthetic proxies, and structural validity metrics for constrained fashion outfit generation.

AI.tldr: USCM + LE-MCTS framework achieves SOTA in fashion outfit generation by modeling compatibility and composition intents, using MCTS for constrained item retrieval.
AI.motivation: Fashion outfit generation is challenging due to non-monotonic/implicit aesthetic compatibility and exponentially large combinatorial search spaces from massive item libraries.
AI.method: Formalizes task as Constrained Ensemble Generation (CEG) modeled as finite-horizon deterministic MDP. Proposes Unified Sequential Composition Model (USCM) to jointly model set-level compatibility and latent composition intents, with Latent Expansion Monte Carlo Tree Search (LE-MCTS) for item retrieval balancing local aesthetic synergy and global structural balance.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on Polyvore Outfits dataset with zero-shot evaluation on iFashion and PolyvoreU, excelling in human preference evaluations, automated aesthetic proxies, and structural validity metrics.
AI.conclusion: The USCM + LE-MCTS framework effectively addresses constrained fashion outfit generation by modeling compatibility and composition jointly with MCTS-guided retrieval, demonstrating superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics.

title: Learning to Assemble Novel Structures with Unfamiliar Parts under Semantic Constraints
comment: Accepted to, and to appear in the 20th Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning (NeSy 2026)
summary: This paper describes a neurosymbolic architecture for learning to assemble novel structures using evidence from embodied conversations and task demonstrations. We focus on scenarios where an agent encounters, after deployment, semantic constraints on structures--in other words, constraints as to which part types and features make valid structures--that were not available during training, and where it is initially unaware of the relevant structure and component part concepts. The agent must acquire and exploit such knowledge through user interactions while attempting assembly. We study this setting in a simulated toy truck assembly domain, learning from symbolic evidence encoded in natural language and from dense visual observations. Our experiments show that communicating semantic constraints through natural language (e.g., "dump trucks have a dumper") yields more data-efficient online adaptation than relying only on task demonstrations and/or only naming the parts through natural language.

AI.tldr: A neurosymbolic architecture learns to assemble novel structures from embodied conversations and demonstrations, handling semantic constraints encountered after deployment through natural language communication.
AI.motivation: Agents deployed in the real world often encounter new semantic constraints about valid structures that weren't available during training, and need to learn these constraints online through interactions while performing assembly tasks.
AI.method: Neurosymbolic architecture combining neural networks with symbolic reasoning, learning from embodied conversations (natural language) and task demonstrations in a simulated toy truck assembly domain. The agent processes both symbolic natural language evidence and dense visual observations.
AI.result: Communicating semantic constraints through natural language (e.g., "dump trucks have a dumper") yields more data-efficient online adaptation than relying only on task demonstrations or only naming parts through natural language.
AI.conclusion: Natural language communication of semantic constraints enables more efficient online learning and adaptation for assembly tasks compared to demonstration-only approaches, supporting the value of combined neural-symbolic approaches for embodied learning.

title: MedMix: Specialization-Consistent Federated Sparse MoEs under Modality Heterogeneity
summary: Federated multimodal medical AI faces modality heterogeneity at both the client and sample levels: clients may systematically lack access to specific modality types, while individual records within the same client may contain different partial modality subsets. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are a promising remedy for modality-adaptive computation, but their use in federated learning is fragile under cross-client modality heterogeneity, where locally learned routing policies can diverge across clients and drive experts toward incompatible specializations. Different clients may assign the same observed modality configuration to different experts, or train similarly indexed experts on different missing-modality configurations, causing standard aggregation to misalign or overwrite the expert specialization that sparse MoEs are intended to learn. To address this challenge, we propose MedMix, a semantic-alignment framework for federated multimodal sparse MoEs that coordinates cross-client routing and expert specialization using modality context. At the client side, MedMix uses modality-context-aware routing to guide expert selection using each token's modality identity, position, and incompleteness context. Across clients, it uses consensus-guided routing alignment to construct server-side consensus anchors for shared modality patterns and align local routing distributions across clients. Complementing these routing mechanisms, client-adaptive expert aggregation leverages client-specific modality-pattern prototypes to match and aggregate functionally similar experts across clients. Experiments on real-world multimodal medical datasets show that MedMix achieves the best average F1 across diverse modality heterogeneity and modality incompleteness settings, with especially clear gains under severe heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: MedMix: A semantic-alignment framework for federated multimodal medical AI that addresses client and sample-level modality heterogeneity through modality-context-aware routing, consensus-guided routing alignment, and client-adaptive expert aggregation.
AI.motivation: Federated multimodal medical AI faces two levels of modality heterogeneity: (1) clients systematically lacking access to specific modality types, and (2) individual records within clients having different partial modality subsets. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are promising but fragile under cross-client modality heterogeneity, causing routing policy divergence and incompatible expert specializations.
AI.method: MedMix introduces three key components: (1) modality-context-aware routing at client side using token's modality identity, position, and incompleteness context; (2) consensus-guided routing alignment across clients using server-side consensus anchors for shared modality patterns; (3) client-adaptive expert aggregation using client-specific modality-pattern prototypes to match and aggregate functionally similar experts.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world multimodal medical datasets show MedMix achieves the best average F1 across diverse modality heterogeneity and modality incompleteness settings, with especially clear gains under severe heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: MedMix effectively addresses the challenges of federated multimodal medical AI under modality heterogeneity by coordinating cross-client routing and expert specialization through semantic alignment mechanisms, improving performance particularly in severely heterogeneous settings.

title: Coverage Aware Active Evaluation for Failure Discovery with Paired Systems
comment: 9 main pages followed by Appendix, total 21 pages, 12 figures
summary: Autonomous systems can fail in rare and heterogeneous ways, making real-world failure discovery difficult under limited testing budgets. Although cheaper proxies such as simulators, lower-fidelity systems, or related policies can be sampled extensively to find failures, proxy failures often do not transfer to the real world due to sim-to-real and system-to-system gaps. The key challenge is therefore to effectively leverage proxy system information for accurate prediction of severe target system failures. We propose an adaptive failure discovery method that combines proxy evaluations with limited target system results to guide scenario selection for target system testing. Our method learns a local predictor of target risk by correcting proxy failure signals using control-variate-inspired residual modeling. To find failures that are both likely and diverse, we combine this predictor with a support-aware mutual-information objective that favors realistic, well-supported regions while expanding coverage across failure modes.
