Across autonomous driving, manipulation, and quadruped velocity-tracking tasks, our method discovers up to 2$\times$ as many failures as random sampling and active-learning baselines, including severe and diverse failures missed by competing methods.

AI.tldr: Adaptive failure discovery method combines proxy system evaluations with limited target system testing to efficiently find severe, diverse real-world failures in autonomous systems.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems fail in rare and heterogeneous ways that are difficult to discover with limited real-world testing budgets. While cheaper proxies (simulators, lower-fidelity systems) can be sampled extensively, their failures often don't transfer to the real world due to sim-to-real and system-to-system gaps.
AI.method: Proposes an adaptive failure discovery method that learns a local predictor of target risk by correcting proxy failure signals using control-variate-inspired residual modeling. Combines this predictor with a support-aware mutual-information objective to find failures that are both likely and diverse, favoring realistic, well-supported regions while expanding coverage across failure modes.
AI.result: The method discovers up to 2× as many failures as random sampling and active-learning baselines across autonomous driving, manipulation, and quadruped velocity-tracking tasks, including severe and diverse failures missed by competing methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive failure discovery approach effectively leverages proxy system information to accurately predict severe target system failures, significantly outperforming baseline methods in discovering diverse and severe real-world failures across multiple autonomous system domains.

title: Hybrid Quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Privacy-Aware Federated Biosignal Learning
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings are sensitive biomedical data, limiting the ability of hospitals and wearable devices to share raw signals for centralized model training. Federated learning addresses this practical privacy constraint by enabling collaborative model training while keeping raw biosignal data at their respective sources. However, federated ECG classification remains challenging due to limited client-side samples, imbalanced arrhythmia labels, and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across clients. These constraints require classifiers that are both communication-efficient and robust to cross-client distribution shifts. In this work, we evaluate a hybrid quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network (HQKAN) against a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for five-class arrhythmia classification on the MIT-BIH dataset and three-class classification on the INCART dataset under federated averaging (FedAvg). Across multiple client configurations, HQKAN improves most aggregate and minority-class metrics while using 37.35% fewer trainable parameters and reducing communication cost by 24.89% on MIT-BIH; on INCART, it achieves corresponding reductions of 44.81% and 36.41%. These results indicate that HQKAN offers a compact, communication-efficient and robust alternative to the MLP baseline for privacy-aware federated learning on biosignal data.

AI.tldr: HQKAN (hybrid quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network) outperforms MLP for federated ECG classification with fewer parameters and lower communication costs while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: ECG data privacy concerns limit centralized model training in healthcare. Federated learning addresses privacy but faces challenges with limited client data, imbalanced arrhythmia labels, and non-IID data distributions across clients.
AI.method: The authors evaluate HQKAN against MLP for five-class arrhythmia classification on MIT-BIH dataset and three-class classification on INCART dataset using federated averaging (FedAvg) across multiple client configurations.
AI.result: HQKAN improves most aggregate and minority-class metrics while using 37.35% fewer parameters and reducing communication cost by 24.89% on MIT-BIH. On INCART, it achieves 44.81% parameter reduction and 36.41% communication cost reduction.
AI.conclusion: HQKAN offers a compact, communication-efficient, and robust alternative to MLP for privacy-aware federated learning on biosignal data, addressing key challenges in federated ECG classification.

title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Pre-registered analysis plan; code and results available
summary:
The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions. Mechanistic interpretability is the obvious source of such evidence, and circuit discovery is its most developed instrument. We ask whether that evidence survives the condition under which it would be relied upon: two competent analysts, the same system, the same tool, different defensible settings.
  We pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, every level taken from a published implementation, and mapped each discovered circuit through a deterministic claim map to a structured Annex IV statement. Across 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task, of which 7,561 produced a claim, the derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738) and the modal claim commands 41.1% of the space. The evidence fails a filability criterion at every tolerance a conformity assessment body would plausibly accept.
  Standardising the single most influential choice, the evaluation metric, leaves the flip rate at 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim entirely and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286), still above the pre-registered threshold. The circuits underlying these claims are structurally near-disjoint, median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%, and functionally uncorrelated at Cohen's kappa 0.015, so the instability is not one mechanism described in different words.
  We give the filability criterion as a standalone protocol, and we report that one of the seven documented discovery objectives does not execute at all on the library's own canonical task. The study covers one model and one task, and whether the conclusion holds at scale is untested.

AI.tldr: Circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability shows high variability across analytical choices, making it unreliable for meeting EU AI Act documentation requirements due to inconsistent evidence generation.
AI.motivation: The EU AI Act requires technical documentation for high-risk AI systems. Mechanistic interpretability and circuit discovery are potential sources for such evidence, but there's uncertainty about whether this evidence would remain consistent across different analysts using the same system and tools.
AI.method: Pre-registered study with 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small for indirect object identification task. Used seven analytic axes from published implementations, mapped discovered circuits through deterministic claim maps to structured Annex IV statements. Analyzed claim consistency, circuit structural similarity (Jaccard overlap), and functional correlation (Cohen's kappa).
AI.result: Derived statements flipped across 73.2% of specification pairs. Even after standardizing the most influential choice (evaluation metric), flip rate remained at 59.4%. Circuits were structurally near-disjoint (median 4% Jaccard overlap) and functionally uncorrelated (kappa 0.015). The evidence failed filability criteria at all plausible tolerances for conformity assessment.
AI.conclusion: Current circuit discovery methods produce highly unstable evidence that would not meet EU AI Act documentation requirements. The inconsistency is fundamental - not just different descriptions of the same mechanism - and raises concerns about the reliability of mechanistic interpretability for regulatory compliance.

title: High-dimensional nonparametric changepoint detection via low-rank degree-two density projection
comment: 20 pages
summary: Detecting distributional changes in high dimension is difficult when neither the pre-change nor post-change density is parametrically specified. We introduce a representation-based approach that retains all degree-at-most-two density information while replacing density estimation by matrix mean estimation. For observations in $[-1,1]^d$, a symmetric feature matrix $H_2(X)\in\R^{(d+1)\times(d+1)}$ is constructed so that $M(f)=\E_f H_2(X)$ is an isometric encoding of the degree-two orthogonal projection of the density. We scan matrix CUSUMs after rank-$r$ truncation, exploiting the low rank of the projected jump rather than sparsity of individual coordinates. The resulting \LRD{} estimator has a tent-shaped population objective and a nonasymptotic operator-norm analysis whose leading stochastic term scales as $\sqrt{rd\log(nd)}$. For multiple changes, we give a seeded narrowest-over-threshold procedure and prove exact recovery by an induction that preserves an isolating interval for every undetected change. A cross-fitted scalar refinement learns the changing low-rank direction on one fold and localizes on the other, attaining $\widetilde O_{\Pp}(κ^{-2})$ error; a matching Le Cam lower bound shows optimality up to logarithms. A geometrically $β$-mixing extension follows from a dependent matrix Bernstein inequality. Experiments with ambient dimension up to $200$, a three-change $d=100$ sequence, and a $128$-feature human-activity benchmark show that the method remains computationally practical and accurately detects pure dependence changes that are invisible to mean CUSUMs.

AI.tldr: A novel representation-based method for detecting distributional changes in high dimensions using matrix CUSUMs with rank-truncation, avoiding density estimation and focusing on low-rank changes rather than coordinate sparsity.
AI.motivation: Detecting distributional changes in high dimensions is challenging without parametric density specifications, especially when neither pre-change nor post-change densities are known. Existing methods struggle with high-dimensional problems where coordinate-wise sparsity assumptions may not hold.
AI.method: The approach constructs symmetric feature matrices H₂(X) for observations in [-1,1]^d, where M(f)=E_f[H₂(X)] encodes degree-two orthogonal projections of densities. It scans matrix CUSUMs after rank-r truncation, exploiting low-rank structure of projected jumps rather than individual coordinate sparsity. For multiple changes, uses seeded narrowest-over-threshold procedure with cross-fitted scalar refinement to learn changing low-rank directions.
AI.result: The LRD estimator achieves √(rd log(nd)) scaling for leading stochastic term. Cross-fitted refinement attains Õₚ(κ⁻²) error, with matching Le Cam lower bound showing near-optimality. Method handles ambient dimensions up to 200, detects pure dependence changes invisible to mean CUSUMs, and extends to geometrically β-mixing processes.
AI.conclusion: The representation-based approach provides computationally practical and theoretically optimal change detection in high dimensions, effectively capturing distributional changes through low-rank structure rather than coordinate sparsity, with proven recovery guarantees and practical applications on real benchmarks.

title: Simulation-Aware In-Context Policy Improvement for LLM-Aided Analog Layout Refinement
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD 2026)
summary: Analog IC layout design remains a labor-intensive iterative process dominated by simulation-driven refinement. Although end-to-end layout generators accelerate initial placement and routing, they still require experts to manually tune layout optimization parameters with repeated post-layout simulations for stringent design specifications. While Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely adopted for parameter tuning in analog IC design, at the layout level it typically requires hundreds to thousands of evaluations, each involving costly parasitic extraction and post-layout simulation, which makes it impractical. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in improving the sample efficiency of such simulation-driven tuning. However, their restricted access to geometric layout context and design-specific heuristics limits their ability to manipulate the layout optimization process. In this paper, we propose a simulation-aware LLM multi-agent framework that performs in-context policy improvement (ICPI) by iteratively updating layout optimization parameters exposed by an analog layout generator through an act-observe-reflect loop on compact structured layout representations. Experiments on real-world analog circuits show that, with only tens of post-layout simulations, our approach improves post-layout performance over the generator's built-in heuristics and BO-based tuning method.

AI.tldr: LLM multi-agent framework with in-context policy improvement tunes analog IC layout parameters using only tens of simulations instead of hundreds/thousands, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Analog IC layout design is labor-intensive with slow simulation-driven refinement. Current methods like Bayesian Optimization require hundreds to thousands of costly post-layout simulations, making them impractical. LLMs show promise for improving sample efficiency but lack proper geometric layout context and design-specific heuristics to effectively manipulate layout optimization.
AI.method: Proposes a simulation-aware LLM multi-agent framework that performs in-context policy improvement (ICPI). The framework iteratively updates layout optimization parameters through an act-observe-reflect loop on compact structured layout representations exposed by an analog layout generator.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world analog circuits show the approach improves post-layout performance over the generator's built-in heuristics and BO-based tuning method, achieving this with only tens of post-layout simulations instead of hundreds/thousands.
AI.conclusion: The LLM multi-agent framework with in-context policy improvement provides a practical, sample-efficient solution for analog IC layout optimization, significantly reducing the simulation burden while outperforming existing automated tuning methods.

title: CForce: Boosting Parallel Decoding for dLLMs via Consistency Forcing
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) accelerate language generation by predicting multiple masks in a single forward pass. However, existing dLLMs can suffer from unreliable predictions in early denoising stages under aggressive parallelism strategies, leading to errors that can propagate to later stages. To tackle this issue, we present Consistency Forcing (CForce) for dLLMs, a distillation method to force the mask predictions of early stages to align with those of later stages. CForce trains the model on pre-collected self-rollout trajectories, thereby improving training-inference alignment. We introduce Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence as a distillation objective to conjoin the merits of forward and reverse KL. We further provide a theoretical analysis for the consistency objective to explain why CForce can approximately minimize the prediction error of early stages. Critically, the same formulation applies to both mask-to-token decoding and edit-capable decoding; in the edit-capable case, later token-to-token refinements provide additional supervision for earlier masked-state predictions. Experiments on non-edit and edit-capable LLaDA models show improved speed-quality trade-offs, especially under high-parallelism decoding budgets. Code is available at: https://github.com/inclusionAI/dFactory.

AI.tldr: CForce is a distillation method for diffusion LLMs that forces early-stage mask predictions to align with later-stage ones using confidence-adaptive KL divergence, improving speed-quality trade-offs in high-parallelism decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion LLMs suffer from unreliable predictions in early denoising stages under aggressive parallelism strategies, causing errors that propagate to later stages, which limits their acceleration benefits.
AI.method: Proposes Consistency Forcing (CForce) - a distillation method that trains models on pre-collected self-rollout trajectories using Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence, which combines forward and reverse KL. The method forces early-stage mask predictions to align with later-stage predictions, with theoretical analysis showing it minimizes early-stage prediction error.
AI.result: Experiments on non-edit and edit-capable LLaDA models show improved speed-quality trade-offs, especially under high-parallelism decoding budgets. The method works for both mask-to-token and edit-capable decoding.
AI.conclusion: CForce effectively addresses the reliability issue of diffusion LLMs in early denoising stages, enabling better acceleration through parallelism while maintaining generation quality, with applicability to both standard and edit-capable decoding scenarios.

title: FLARE MCMC: Fidelity-based Layer-Adaptive REcursive proposals for MCMC
comment: This is the author's accepted manuscript of an article published in SIAM Journal on Uncertainty Quantification. The final version is available at \url{https://doi.org/10.1137/25M1795194
summary: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) requires only the ability to evaluate the likelihood, making it a common technique for inference in complex models. However, it can have a slow mixing rate, requiring the generation of many samples to obtain good estimates and an overall high computational cost. FLARE MCMC is a multi-fidelity layered MCMC method that exploits lower-fidelity approximations of the true likelihood calculation to improve mixing and leads to overall faster performance. Such lower-fidelity likelihoods are commonly available in scientific and engineering applications where the model involves a simulation whose resolution or accuracy can be tuned. Our technique uses recursive, layered chains with simple layer tuning; it does not require the likelihood to take any form or have any particular internal mathematical structure. We demonstrate experimentally that FLARE MCMC achieves larger effective sample sizes for the same computational time across different scientific domains including hydrology and cosmology.

AI.tldr: FLARE MCMC is a multi-fidelity layered MCMC method that uses lower-fidelity likelihood approximations to improve mixing rates and computational efficiency, achieving better effective sample sizes across scientific domains.
AI.motivation: Standard MCMC methods can have slow mixing rates, requiring many samples and high computational cost, especially for complex models with expensive likelihood evaluations. Many scientific applications have models where simulation resolution/accuracy can be tuned, providing natural lower-fidelity approximations.
AI.method: FLARE MCMC uses a multi-fidelity layered approach with recursive chains that exploit lower-fidelity approximations of the true likelihood calculation. The method features simple layer tuning and doesn't require the likelihood to have any particular mathematical structure or form.
AI.result: Experimental demonstrations show FLARE MCMC achieves larger effective sample sizes for the same computational time compared to standard methods. This improvement is demonstrated across different scientific domains including hydrology and cosmology.
AI.conclusion: FLARE MCMC provides a practical solution to slow MCMC mixing by leveraging available lower-fidelity likelihood approximations, leading to significant computational efficiency gains without requiring special likelihood structures, making it broadly applicable in scientific computing.

title: Post-training Quantization for Hybrid Iterative Generative Models
summary: Iterative Generative Models (IGMs) span autoregressive and diffusion paradigms, and hybrid variants that couple them can achieve remarkable image-generation fidelity. However, their iterative inference incurs substantial computational overhead, making Post-training Quantization (PTQ) appealing for acceleration, while directly applying vanilla PTQ to hybrid IGMs can trigger model collapse. By analyzing these failures, we identify two critical challenges: Excessive Outliers (EOs) in the activations create an irreconcilable trade-off between preserving normal precision and covering EOs, resulting in severe degradation in generation quality; Amplified Anomalies (AAs) arising unpredictably from minor quantization errors, create a mismatch between calibration and inference, thus iteratively triggering model collapse. To address these challenges, we introduce HyGenQ, a PTQ framework for hybrid IGMs. HyGenQ comprises Hierarchical Cluster Decoupling (HCD) and Scaling Recalibration (SR). HCD identifies and decouples outlier channels via a multi-stage clustering process, effectively isolating EOs while maintaining normal value precision, thereby alleviating performance degradation. SR scales AAs beyond Gaussian Bound, thereby avoiding model collapse caused by aggressive truncation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HyGenQ successfully quantizes representative hybrid IGMs to 8-bit precision (W8A8), significantly outperforming existing baselines and validating its robustness across different model families.

AI.tldr: HyGenQ is a post-training quantization framework for hybrid iterative generative models that addresses excessive outliers and amplified anomalies through hierarchical cluster decoupling and scaling recalibration, enabling robust 8-bit quantization while preserving generation quality.
AI.motivation: Hybrid iterative generative models achieve remarkable image-generation fidelity but have substantial computational overhead due to iterative inference. While post-training quantization is appealing for acceleration, vanilla PTQ approaches cause model collapse in these hybrid models due to excessive outliers and amplified anomalies.
AI.method: HyGenQ introduces two main techniques: 1) Hierarchical Cluster Decoupling (HCD) - identifies and decouples outlier channels via multi-stage clustering to isolate excessive outliers while maintaining normal value precision. 2) Scaling Recalibration (SR) - scales amplified anomalies beyond Gaussian bounds to avoid model collapse from aggressive truncation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show HyGenQ successfully quantizes representative hybrid iterative generative models to 8-bit precision (W8A8), significantly outperforming existing baselines and validating robustness across different model families.
AI.conclusion: The HyGenQ framework effectively addresses the critical challenges of excessive outliers and amplified anomalies in hybrid iterative generative models, enabling practical post-training quantization to 8-bit precision without model collapse or severe degradation in generation quality.

title: Probabilistic indirect models for undrained shear strength: addressing significant data missing and variability with advanced imputation and machine learning techniques
summary: Accurate prediction of undrained shear strength (su) is crucial for geotechnical design, but is often hampered by substantial uncertainty in traditional empirical methods. This study uses the CLAY/10/7490 global database to develop probabilistic indirect models to predict su based on Atterberg limits and piezocone cone penetration (CPTU) measurements. Firstly, the dataset has a high missing data rate and variability. We test three imputation methods - multivariate normal (MN), multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), and miss forest (MF) - to fill the missing values. To validate their effectiveness, a Probabilistic Extreme Gradient Boosting (PXGB) model is developed, and the imputation methods are evaluated by comparing the PXGB's performance when trained on the imputed datasets against that on the original incomplete data. Secondly, the indirect model is built by integrating a multi-head attention (MHA) mechanism into an artificial neural network (ANN) to enhance information extraction from limited data, which leads to the MHA-based probabilistic neural networks (MHA-PNN) model. The models' performance, alongside a conventional MN-based prediction model, was evaluated using root mean square error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), conditional interval width (wCI), and coverage rate (CR). Results demonstrate that the proposed MN-enhanced MHA-PNN model substantially outperforms other models in both prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification. These findings highlight the potential of this integrated strategy for building robust probabilistic indirect models in geotechnical applications, particularly when confronted with sparse and incomplete datasets.

AI.tldr: Proposes MN-enhanced MHA-PNN model for probabilistic prediction of undrained shear strength using Atterberg limits and CPTU data, combining missing data imputation with attention-based neural networks.
AI.motivation: Substantial uncertainty in traditional empirical methods for predicting undrained shear strength (su) hampers geotechnical design accuracy. There's a need for robust probabilistic models that can handle sparse and incomplete geotechnical datasets effectively.
AI.method: 1) Evaluated three imputation methods (MN, MICE, MF) on CLAY/10/7490 database with high missing data. 2) Developed Probabilistic Extreme Gradient Boosting (PXGB) model to validate imputation effectiveness. 3) Built indirect prediction model using multi-head attention (MHA) mechanism integrated into artificial neural network (ANN), creating MHA-based probabilistic neural networks (MHA-PNN). Compared against conventional MN-based prediction model using RMSE, R², MAPE, wCI, and CR metrics.
AI.result: The proposed MN-enhanced MHA-PNN model substantially outperforms other models in both prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification. The integrated strategy effectively handles sparse and incomplete datasets while providing robust probabilistic predictions.
AI.conclusion: The integrated strategy combining missing data imputation with attention-based neural networks has significant potential for building robust probabilistic indirect models in geotechnical applications, particularly when dealing with sparse and incomplete datasets.

title: SDO: Subspace Deconflicting Operator for Multi-Adapter Composition
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted by ACM MM 2026 Main Track
summary: Composing independently trained adapters within a shared diffusion backbone provides a modular approach to multi-character generation, but naive joint deployment often causes identity mixing, cross-character attribute leakage, and unstable scene composition. We study this interference from a parameter-space perspective and hypothesize that it arises partly from conflicts between overlapping dominant subspaces in shared layers. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SDO}, a \textbf{S}ubspace \textbf{D}econflicting \textbf{O}perator for multi-adapter composition. SDO reconstructs layer-wise low-rank updates from the selected adapters, extracts compact subspace signatures, measures pairwise conflict through output-subspace overlap, and applies a permutation-equivariant transformation that suppresses harmful shared directions while retaining identity-specific characteristics. The resulting representations are mapped back to standard adapter updates and can be directly incorporated into existing diffusion inference pipelines. Experiments demonstrate that SDO consistently improves identity fidelity and compositional stability, with particularly clear gains as the number of jointly composed adapters increases.

AI.tldr: SDO is a subspace deconflicting operator that reduces interference when composing multiple adapters in diffusion models for multi-character generation.
AI.motivation: When independently trained adapters are composed in shared diffusion backbones for multi-character generation, naive joint deployment causes identity mixing, attribute leakage, and unstable scene composition due to parameter-space interference.
AI.method: SDO reconstructs layer-wise low-rank updates from selected adapters, extracts compact subspace signatures, measures pairwise conflict through output-subspace overlap, and applies a permutation-equivariant transformation that suppresses harmful shared directions while retaining identity-specific characteristics.
AI.result: SDO consistently improves identity fidelity and compositional stability, with particularly clear gains as the number of jointly composed adapters increases.
AI.conclusion: SDO effectively addresses interference in multi-adapter composition by identifying and suppressing conflicting parameter subspaces, enabling better multi-character generation while maintaining each character's identity-specific characteristics.

title: Polar Code Based Federated Learning: Convergence Analysis and Resource Allocation
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed devices without sharing raw data; however, it faces significant communication bottlenecks and channel impairments in practice. Conventional network layer treatments either idealize the channel as error free or apply equal error protection (EEP) to transmitted model updates, failing to account for the inherently unequal importance of quantization bits within a single local model. To address this limitation, we propose a cross layer polar code based FL scheme that leverages the unequal error protection (UEP) property of polar codes under finite block lengths. Specifically, the proposed design selectively protects more significant quantization bits, thereby mitigating the detrimental effects of channel noise. We further provide a rigorous convergence analysis of the proposed scheme, deriving an upper bound on the convergence gap, which we then jointly optimize over the number of quantization bits and the polar code block length across all training iterations. Experimental results demonstrate that both constant and variable block length configurations of our polar code based scheme consistently achieve substantial performance gains over uncoded and LDPC-based EEP benchmarks, with the advantage becoming increasingly pronounced as the channel quality deteriorating. These findings confirm the efficacy of our cross-layer design in enhancing FL robustness and efficiency under realistic channel conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a cross-layer polar code based federated learning scheme that uses unequal error protection to selectively protect more significant quantization bits, improving FL robustness under realistic channel conditions.
AI.motivation: Federated learning faces significant communication bottlenecks and channel impairments. Conventional approaches either idealize channels as error-free or apply equal error protection to model updates, failing to account for the unequal importance of quantization bits within local models.
AI.method: The authors propose a cross-layer design leveraging polar codes' unequal error protection property under finite block lengths. They selectively protect more significant quantization bits and provide rigorous convergence analysis with joint optimization over quantization bits and polar code block length across training iterations.
AI.result: Both constant and variable block length configurations of the polar code scheme consistently achieve substantial performance gains over uncoded and LDPC-based equal error protection benchmarks, with advantages becoming more pronounced as channel quality deteriorates.
AI.conclusion: The cross-layer polar code based scheme effectively enhances federated learning robustness and efficiency under realistic channel conditions by exploiting the unequal importance of model quantization bits through selective protection.

title: Joint Optimization of Memory and Computing Frequency for Energy-Efficient DNN Inference
summary: Deep neural network (DNN) inference on mobile devices often incurs high latency and energy consumption due to limited computing and memory resources. To enable energy-efficient DNN inference, most existing studies focus on dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) for adjusting the computing frequency, while the impact of memory frequency on the inference performance has been greatly overlooked. In this paper, we consider the impact of memory frequency and computing frequency on DNN inference time, and jointly optimize these two frequencies together with communication resources for energy-efficient DNN inference. Based on a realistic inference time model, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the energy consumption of all mobile devices under the deadline constraint. For local inference, we derive a near-optimal closed-form solution via convex optimization, while an optimal closed-form solution for transmission power is obtained for edge inference with the given bandwidth. Furthermore, we propose a low-complexity heuristic algorithm to effectively solve the overall problem with polynomial time complexity. Simulation results based on measured data show that the proposed near-optimal solution for local inference can achieve optimal performance under strict deadline constraints, with a performance gap of up to 2.5% compared with the optimal solution. Meanwhile, our proposed algorithm significantly reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 10.4% compared to other methods.

AI.tldr: Joint optimization of computing and memory frequencies with communication resources for energy-efficient DNN inference on mobile devices under deadline constraints.
AI.motivation: Deep neural network inference on mobile devices suffers from high latency and energy consumption due to limited resources. Existing studies focus primarily on dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) for computing frequency, while overlooking the impact of memory frequency on inference performance.
AI.method: Proposes a joint optimization of both computing frequency and memory frequency with communication resources. Develops a realistic inference time model and formulates an optimization problem to minimize energy consumption under deadline constraints. For local inference, derives a near-optimal closed-form solution via convex optimization. For edge inference, obtains optimal closed-form solution for transmission power given bandwidth. Also proposes a low-complexity heuristic algorithm with polynomial time complexity.
AI.result: Simulation results based on measured data show that the near-optimal solution for local inference achieves optimal performance under strict deadline constraints with up to 2.5% performance gap compared to optimal solution. The proposed algorithm reduces device energy consumption by up to 10.4% compared to other methods.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of computing frequency, memory frequency, and communication resources is crucial for energy-efficient DNN inference on mobile devices. The proposed approach effectively addresses the overlooked impact of memory frequency and provides practical solutions with significant energy savings.

title: QUASAR: Lowering the Loss Floor of Quantization-Aware Training with Loss-Aware Reconstruction
comment: 39 pages
summary: As large language model inference shifts toward lower precision, post-training quantization (PTQ) becomes increasingly brittle, making quantization-aware training (QAT) essential for preserving model quality. However, QAT computes the loss and surrogate gradients using a lossy reconstruction of latent full-precision weights, while applying updates to the latent weights themselves. This mismatch can lead to suboptimal training trajectories and a higher loss floor. Second-order PTQ methods mitigate a similar gap by minimizing loss-aware reconstruction error, but doing it once for a frozen model can take hours; repeating this process throughout QAT as the weights evolve is impractical. We introduce QUASAR, a QAT method that continuously performs lightweight, loss-aware reconstruction in the training loop to lower the loss floor and improve the resulting low-bit model. At each training step, QUASAR uses the exponential moving average of squared gradients as online saliency estimates, searches over a small set of clipping ranges, and fits affine dequantizers via saliency-weighted least squares. Our analysis shows that the loss-aware reconstruction error is the only reconstruction-dependent term in the QAT convergence bound and controls the loss of the final quantized model, establishing QUASAR's objective as a principled optimization target. QUASAR modifies only the training procedure and supports standard deployment formats, including integer quantization and NVFP4, with no inference-time changes or overhead. Across Qwen3 and Llama-3.1, QUASAR achieves the lowest held-out KL divergence among competitive QAT methods at 2, 3, and 4 bits, reducing KL by at least 10% at 3 and 4 bits and by 29% at 2 bits. At 2 bits, it improves average accuracy across eight tasks by 3.5-4.3 percentage points over strong QAT and PTQ baselines.

AI.tldr: QUASAR introduces a lightweight, loss-aware reconstruction method for quantization-aware training that continuously optimizes clipping ranges and affine dequantizers during training to lower the loss floor and improve low-bit model performance.
AI.motivation: As LLM inference shifts to lower precision, post-training quantization becomes brittle, making quantization-aware training essential. However, QAT has a fundamental mismatch: it computes loss using quantized weights but applies updates to full-precision latent weights, leading to suboptimal training trajectories and higher loss floors.
AI.method: QUASAR performs continuous lightweight loss-aware reconstruction during QAT. At each training step, it uses exponential moving averages of squared gradients as online saliency estimates, searches over a small set of clipping ranges, and fits affine dequantizers via saliency-weighted least squares. It modifies only the training procedure and supports standard deployment formats.
AI.result: Across Qwen3 and Llama-3.1, QUASAR achieves the lowest held-out KL divergence among competitive QAT methods at 2, 3, and 4 bits, reducing KL by at least 10% at 3/4 bits and by 29% at 2 bits. At 2 bits, it improves average accuracy across eight tasks by 3.5-4.3 percentage points over strong QAT and PTQ baselines.
AI.conclusion: QUASAR provides a principled, lightweight approach to loss-aware reconstruction during QAT that significantly improves model quality at low bit precision without inference overhead, making it practical for real-world deployment of quantized LLMs.

title: MemoryLake on MemoryArena: A Matched Study of Agent Memory Backends
comment: 16 pages, 7 tables
summary: Most agent-memory benchmarks test post-hoc recall, whereas MemoryArena evaluates whether memory supports interdependent, multi-session task completion. We compare MemoryLake, a structured multi-track memory backend, with Mem0, text-embedding-3-small vector RAG, and a long-context control across all five MemoryArena domains. The systems share the same agent framework, requested gpt-5-mini model alias, task samples, and scoring code; the memory integration is the intentionally changed component. Because each backend bundles write, retrieval, consolidation, budgeting, and prompt-assembly choices, the study is a matched system-level comparison, not a representation-only ablation or a cost-matched experiment. On the shared evaluation sets, MemoryLake has the highest observed success rate (SR) in mathematics (9/40), physics (12/20), and progressive retrieval (4/20). Every system has zero SR in travel planning, and web shopping yields a single bundle-level success (long context, 1/150); MemoryLake ranks third on both the travel soft process score and shopping step match. Following MemoryArena's suite-level convention, a post-hoc equal-weight average over the five SRs is 20.5% for MemoryLake versus 13.6% for the best comparator. These are point estimates: sample sizes are modest, confidence intervals overlap, and we do not report paired significance tests. A separate MemoryLake-only run over all 221 progressive queries yields a failure-counted SR of 26.7% (59/221) and is not a baseline comparison. The results support a workload-dependent view of memory backends and an observed lead among the four evaluated systems on the shared sets; they do not establish benchmark-wide state of the art or a causal advantage of representation structure.

AI.tldr: MemoryArena benchmark evaluates memory backends for multi-session task completion; MemoryLake shows highest success rates in some domains but no system performs well overall.
AI.motivation: Most existing agent-memory benchmarks focus on post-hoc recall rather than evaluating whether memory systems actually support interdependent, multi-session task completion. The paper aims to fill this gap by comparing different memory backend approaches using a more practical evaluation framework.
AI.method: The study compares MemoryLake (structured multi-track memory backend) with Mem0, text-embedding-3-small vector RAG, and a long-context control across five MemoryArena domains. They use identical agent framework, GPT-5-mini model, task samples, and scoring code, with memory integration as the only varied component - making this a matched system-level comparison rather than a representation-only ablation.
AI.result: MemoryLake achieves highest success rates in mathematics (9/40), physics (12/20), and progressive retrieval (4/20). All systems fail in travel planning (0 success), and web shopping yields only one bundle-level success (long context, 1/150). MemoryLake ranks third on travel soft process score and shopping step match. Overall equal-weight average success rate across five domains is 20.5% for MemoryLake vs 13.6% for best comparator.
AI.conclusion: Results support a workload-dependent view of memory backends and show MemoryLake leads among evaluated systems on shared evaluation sets, but don't establish benchmark-wide state-of-the-art or causal advantage of representation structure. The modest sample sizes and overlapping confidence intervals limit strong statistical claims.

title: Identifiability and Order-Dimension Limits of In-Context Learning on Partial Orders
summary: In-context learning is commonly formalized as inference from examples of a function. Partial orders instead combine transitivity, antisymmetry, and incomparability, so a finite prompt may not determine a queried comparison. We develop a theory of in-context learning on partial orders that separates logical identifiability, prompt teaching cost, structural complexity, and the exact capacity of a formal coordinate-decoder class. A version-space semantics makes background knowledge and open- versus closed-world assumptions explicit. For finite open-world prompts with positive and negative comparisons, we prove an exact completion trichotomy: after taking the reflexive transitive closure of the positive demonstrations, a query is forced true, forced false because every true completion creates a cycle or violates a negative demonstration, or remains genuinely ambiguous. For a known $n$-element universe, we characterize the open-world teaching number as the number of covers plus a blocker-set hitting number, prove that its maximum over all $n$-element posets is $n(n-1)$ and is uniquely attained by the antichain, and identify the blocker term as the exact cost of open-world rather than complete-Hasse semantics. We formalize prompt-dependent $s$-coordinate decoders and use the classical coordinate-order equivalence to obtain an exact representation boundary: dimension at most $s$ is necessary and sufficient, while width at most $s$ is a convenient sufficient condition.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a formal theory of in-context learning for partial orders, analyzing when queries can be logically determined from finite prompts and characterizing the exact computational boundaries.
AI.motivation: Partial orders present unique challenges for in-context learning because unlike functions, they involve transitivity, antisymmetry, and incomparability relations. A finite prompt may not uniquely determine a queried comparison, creating ambiguity that requires formal analysis.
AI.method: Develops a theory using version-space semantics to separate logical identifiability, teaching cost, and structural complexity. Analyzes open-world prompts with positive/negative comparisons, proves a trichotomy theorem for completion, characterizes teaching numbers, and formalizes prompt-dependent coordinate decoders using classical coordinate-order equivalence.
AI.result: Proves an exact completion trichotomy: queries are forced true, forced false (due to cycle creation or negative violation), or genuinely ambiguous. Characterizes open-world teaching number as covers plus blocker-set hitting number, shows maximum is n(n-1) attained by antichain, and establishes dimension ≤ s as necessary/sufficient representation boundary.
AI.conclusion: The theory provides precise boundaries for in-context learning on partial orders, separating different aspects of complexity and establishing exact relationships between structural properties and learning capacity in both open-world and closed-world settings.

title: When Personal Memory Has No Single Answer: Evaluating LLM Agents under Irreducible Conflict
summary: LLM agents increasingly maintain personal memory across sessions, but it can conflict. Preferences depend on context, behavior evolves, and sources can conflict. When a query lacks context, time, or source authority to interpret conflict, treating one memory as definitive converts unresolved conflict into an unjustified, overconfident action. Existing benchmarks recover one answer from conflicting evidence, overlooking whether agents recognize underdetermination, preserve alternatives, seek missing information, and choose appropriate actions. We introduce \underline{T}esting \underline{A}gents' \underline{N}avigation of \underline{G}enuine, \underline{L}atent, and \underline{E}ntangled Memory Conflicts (\textsc{TANGLE}), a benchmark for genuinely unresolvable memory conflicts. It comprises 541 instances across 40 personas and three types: Context-Partitioned Conflict (CPC), Behavior-Oscillation Conflict (BOC), and Source-Contradiction Conflict (SCC). We evaluate two tracks---an oracle track with curated memory and a pipeline track that extracts memory from multi-session dialogues---on five dimensions: conflict perception, causal reasoning, confidence calibration, clarification seeking, and memory faithfulness. Experiments reveal pipeline challenges. With curated memory, models recognize conflicts more reliably than they calibrate actions or seek targeted clarification. With end-to-end pipeline memory, extraction fails to preserve conflict-bearing relations needed for downstream reasoning. Policy comparisons show fixed rules are insufficient when actions must reflect conflict. These findings motivate Conflict-Aware Action Policy (CAAP), which adapts actions to each conflict using available evidence. \textsc{TANGLE} frames conflict handling as recognizing underdetermination, retaining conflicting evidence, and acting without forcing a definitive answer.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (TANGLE) for testing how LLM agents handle genuinely unresolvable memory conflicts, evaluating their ability to recognize underdetermination, preserve alternatives, seek information, and choose appropriate actions rather than forcing definitive answers.
AI.motivation: LLM agents maintain personal memory across sessions, but these memories can conflict in various ways (context-dependent preferences, evolving behaviors, conflicting sources). When queries lack sufficient context, temporal information, or source authority to resolve conflicts, treating one memory as definitive leads to unjustified, overconfident actions. Existing benchmarks focus on recovering one answer from conflicting evidence, failing to test whether agents properly handle underdetermination.
AI.method: Created the TANGLE benchmark with 541 instances across 40 personas and three conflict types: Context-Partitioned Conflict (CPC), Behavior-Oscillation Conflict (BOC), and Source-Contradiction Conflict (SCC). Evaluated two tracks: an oracle track with curated memory and a pipeline track extracting memory from multi-session dialogues. Assessed five dimensions: conflict perception, causal reasoning, confidence calibration, clarification seeking, and memory faithfulness. Proposed Conflict-Aware Action Policy (CAAP) that adapts actions based on available evidence.
AI.result: With curated memory, models recognize conflicts more reliably than they calibrate actions or seek targeted clarification. With end-to-end pipeline memory, extraction fails to preserve conflict-bearing relations needed for downstream reasoning. Policy comparisons show fixed rules are insufficient when actions must reflect conflict. The CAAP approach shows promise by adapting actions to each conflict type using available evidence.
AI.conclusion: TANGLE frames conflict handling as recognizing underdetermination, retaining conflicting evidence, and acting without forcing a definitive answer. The findings highlight the need for better conflict-aware policies in LLM agents and reveal challenges in memory extraction for conflict handling.

title: When Does More Correct Data Hurt? Insertion-Stability and the Limits of Dimension-Based Theory
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure
summary:
Adding data known to be correct ought to be safe. Not always. Larsen, Pabbaraju and Shetty model the failure with a monotone adversary, which reads an i.i.d. training sample and may append as many further examples as it likes, provided the target hypothesis labels them all. Mehrotra has since settled the cost, showing that for classes of VC dimension d >= 2 no learner can guarantee expected error better than Theta((d/n)log(en/d)), a logarithmic factor above the clean PAC rate.
  Because that rate is a worst case over all classes, it says nothing about which classes actually suffer the penalty, and the answer turns on the learner. We call a learner insertion-stable if feeding it more correctly labeled examples can only shrink the region where it errs. Such learners are immune to the adversary, since on any given sample the risk after insertions never exceeds the risk on the clean part alone, however much is added and however cleverly it is chosen. High- probability guarantees carry over unchanged, and because Closure is insertion-stable every intersection-closed class keeps its clean rate of E[Err] <= (21d+34)/n.
  Immunity is not something the classical dimensions can predict. Two classes can agree on VCdim = Ldim = 2 and still split, one at Theta(1/n) and the other at Theta(log(en)/n), while intervals have unbounded Littlestone dimension and are immune anyway. On Mehrotra's hard class we prove more than the failure of a single algorithm, showing that no monotone permutation-invariant compression scheme of any finite size attains the clean rate.
  The question is therefore not whether a class is hard, nor whether a learner is good, but whether the two suit each other. Given an insertion-stable learner that is optimal on clean data, correct additions are free, and without one the cost belongs to the class, so changing the learner will not avoid it.

AI.tldr: Adding correctly labeled data should help learning but isn't always safe due to monotone adversaries, though insertion-stable learners can avoid this penalty and maintain clean PAC rates.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a counterintuitive phenomenon where adding correctly labeled data can actually hurt learning performance when an adversary strategically adds more examples. This challenges the assumption that more correct data is always beneficial, and explores which learners and hypothesis classes are vulnerable to this attack.
AI.method: The paper introduces the concept of "insertion-stable" learners whose error regions only shrink with additional correctly labeled data. It analyzes which classes can be learned by such stable learners, proving immunity results for intersection-closed classes, and establishes lower bounds showing that without insertion stability, the adversary can force a logarithmic penalty above the clean PAC rate.
AI.result: Key findings: 1) Insertion-stable learners maintain clean PAC rates (E[Err] ≤ (21d+34)/n for intersection-closed classes) despite adversarial additions, 2) Classical dimensions (VC, Littlestone) cannot predict vulnerability - classes with same dimensions can have different vulnerability, 3) No monotone permutation-invariant compression scheme of finite size achieves the clean rate on Mehrotra's hard class, 4) Vulnerability depends on the match between learner and class, not just one or the other.
AI.conclusion: The security against adversarial data insertion depends on the compatibility between learner stability and hypothesis class structure. Insertion-stable learners paired with suitable classes (like intersection-closed ones) preserve clean learning rates, while mismatched pairs incur logarithmic penalties that are inherent to the class itself, not avoidable by switching learners.

title: Never the Number: Structural Abstention for AI Systems Whose Answers Are Consumed as Fact
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Technical report. Describes architecture and design principles only; contains no code, schemas, datasets, or performance metrics
summary:
Large language models have made natural language interfaces to databases (NLIDB) newly credible, but LLM text-to-SQL systems fail in a way that matters for deployment: a hallucinated column or a mis-aggregated total yields a fluent wrong answer, indistinguishable at the point of use from a right one. Where the consumer cannot inspect the generated query, as in enterprise AI deployments and operational dashboards, and increasingly where the consumer is a tool-using agent rather than a person, accuracy alone is insufficient: nothing marks which answers to distrust. This is a reliability problem before it is an accuracy problem.
  We propose an architectural pattern for such systems, a trusted kernel with a generative shell, resting on one invariant: a component that can fabricate may influence which question the system answers, never which value it returns. A generative shell interprets underspecified input and phrases replies; a deterministic kernel matches fully specified questions against a bounded set of answerable question shapes and compiles them to queries by deterministic execution. The two meet at a confirmation the user reads before any value is computed, and requests the kernel cannot express are declined rather than approximated. We call this structural abstention, and distinguish it from the statistical abstention of selective prediction and calibrated confidence: refusal here needs no confidence estimate, because unanswerable requests are unrepresentable.
  We specify the pattern implementation-independently, give a five-decision recipe and work it across three domains, extend the invariant from returned values to the actions of agentic systems, and report a two-year production case study alongside two generative alternatives, a fine-tuned parser and a tool-retrieval agent. We close against enterprise and reliability benchmarks published since.

AI.tldr: A trusted kernel with generative shell architecture for LLM-based database interfaces that prevents hallucination by separating interpretation from query execution, ensuring unanswerable requests are declined rather than approximated.
AI.motivation: LLM text-to-SQL systems generate fluent but potentially wrong answers that users can't distinguish from correct ones, creating a reliability problem for enterprise deployments where accuracy alone is insufficient because there's no way to know which answers to distrust.
AI.method: Proposes a trusted kernel with generative shell architecture: a generative shell interprets underspecified user input and phrases replies, while a deterministic kernel matches fully specified questions against answerable question shapes and compiles queries deterministically. The two meet at a user confirmation before any value computation.
AI.result: The paper specifies the pattern implementation-independently, provides a five-decision recipe, applies it across three domains, extends the invariant to agentic systems, and reports a two-year production case study comparing it against generative alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Structural abstention (declining unanswerable requests rather than approximating them) addresses reliability problems in LLM database interfaces by ensuring fabricated components can influence which question gets answered but never which values get returned.

title: Adversarial Learning of Classifier-Free Guidance Schedules
summary: Modern text-to-image diffusion models rely on classifier-free guidance (CFG) to achieve high image fidelity and text alignment. However, CFG typically applies a static, global scale across all timesteps, samples, and conditions -- a choice that is generally suboptimal and can introduce artifacts, as different states may benefit from different levels of guidance. While time-varying schedules are known to improve quality, designing them by hand is non-trivial and application-dependent. In this paper, we learn the guidance schedule as a function of diffusion time, conditioning and the current noisy sample, in order to better align sampled images with the text prompt. We frame this as a density ratio estimation problem: a discriminator is trained to estimate the time-dependent log-density ratio between the true and guided marginal distributions, while a lightweight generator network predicts the optimal, state-dependent guidance scale. Empirically, our approach outperforms both heuristic CFG schedules and prior methods for learning dynamic guidance on text-to-image generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Learning dynamic, state-dependent guidance scales for text-to-image diffusion models outperforms static classifier-free guidance, improving text alignment and reducing artifacts.
AI.motivation: Static, global classifier-free guidance scales are suboptimal and can introduce artifacts in text-to-image generation, as different states (timesteps, samples, conditions) may benefit from different levels of guidance. While time-varying schedules help, manually designing them is non-trivial and application-dependent.
AI.method: The approach learns guidance schedules as functions of diffusion time, conditioning, and current noisy sample. It frames this as a density ratio estimation problem: training a discriminator to estimate time-dependent log-density ratio between true and guided marginal distributions, while a lightweight generator network predicts optimal state-dependent guidance scales.
AI.result: The method empirically outperforms both heuristic CFG schedules and prior methods for learning dynamic guidance on text-to-image generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, state-dependent guidance scaling learned through density ratio estimation is superior to static guidance for text-to-image diffusion models, leading to better text alignment and image quality.

title: AI Research Preference Models
comment: 34 pages, 17 figures, 6 tables
summary: AI research agents (AIRA) can now propose, implement, and evaluate their own machine learning experiments, but progress on frontier tasks is throttled by cost: a candidate solution can be written in minutes, whereas evaluating it can take hours to days of GPU time. An agent can therefore propose far more candidates than it can afford to run, and its progress depends on its research preference: how it allocates a fixed execution budget across many candidates. We introduce AI Research Preference Models (RPMs) that predict which of multiple candidate solutions are most worth executing, without paying the cost of executing them all. We build RPMs from frozen pretrained language models (with no task-specific training), in two forms: an inference-only model that reasons over candidate plans, code, and prior executed solutions, and an agentic model that additionally runs small-scale pilot experiments before deciding. We integrate both into the AIRA-dojo search agent and evaluate on AIRS-Bench, a recent benchmark of machine learning research tasks for AI research agents. The two variants raise the average normalized score from 0.684 to 0.711 and 0.729 respectively, and reach the unguided agent's 24-hour performance in roughly 15 hours, using less than two-thirds of its execution budget. Our best RPMs also yield new state-of-the-art results on two AIRS-Bench tasks.

AI.tldr: AI Research Preference Models (RPMs) help AI research agents prioritize which candidate solutions to execute first by predicting their potential value, significantly reducing computational costs while maintaining or improving research performance.
AI.motivation: AI research agents can generate candidate solutions much faster than they can evaluate them due to high GPU computation costs, creating a bottleneck where agents propose far more candidates than they can afford to execute within budget constraints.
AI.method: Develop two types of RPMs using frozen pretrained language models: 1) Inference-only model that reasons over candidate plans, code, and prior solutions, and 2) Agentic model that additionally runs small-scale pilot experiments. Both are integrated into the AIRA-dojo search agent framework.
AI.result: RPMs improve average normalized score on AIRS-Bench from 0.684 to 0.711 (inference-only) and 0.729 (agentic). The best RPMs achieve unguided agent's 24-hour performance in ~15 hours using <2/3 of execution budget, and set new SOTA results on two AIRS-Bench tasks.
AI.conclusion: Research Preference Models effectively address the computational bottleneck in AI research agents by enabling smarter budget allocation, significantly accelerating research progress while reducing costs without requiring task-specific training.

title: Model-agnostic Retrieval-Augmented Extended Forecasting for time series
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure
summary: Time series forecasting with pretrained foundation models has demonstrated strong zero-shot capabilities. However, achieving optimal performance on time series with short or negligible historical data in domain-specific applications typically requires adaptation via either fine-tuning or RAG. While fine-tuning is effective, it incurs substantial computational costs. This work explores RAG within univariate time series (Retrieval Augmented Generation) as a more efficient alternative, in particular RAF (Retrieval Augmented Forecasting), and introduces RAEF (Retrieval-Augmented Extended Forecasting), a model-agnostic method built upon RAF. RAEF incorporates key refinements to the retrieval and aggregation mechanisms: (1) direct retrieval in input-space rather than embedding-space, reducing inference overhead, and (2) concatenation-based aggregation that preserves temporal structure instead of averaging. Empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrates that RAEF outperforms RAF in both accuracy and inference overhead. Furthermore, comprehensive comparisons with zero-shot and fine-tuned foundation models show that RAEF achieves competitive or superior performance to fine-tuning while avoiding its computational burden, establishing it as a practical and scalable approach for domain adaptation in time series forecasting.

AI.tldr: RAEF is a retrieval-augmented method for time series forecasting that improves upon RAF with direct input-space retrieval and temporal-preserving aggregation, achieving competitive performance to fine-tuning without the computational cost.
AI.motivation: Foundation models show strong zero-shot time series forecasting capabilities, but domain-specific applications with limited historical data require adaptation. Fine-tuning is effective but computationally expensive, so the paper explores retrieval-augmented methods as a more efficient alternative.
AI.method: Proposes RAEF (Retrieval-Augmented Extended Forecasting), a model-agnostic extension of RAF with two key refinements: 1) direct retrieval in input-space (rather than embedding-space) to reduce inference overhead, and 2) concatenation-based aggregation that preserves temporal structure instead of averaging.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows RAEF outperforms RAF in both accuracy and inference overhead. RAEF achieves competitive or superior performance to fine-tuned foundation models while avoiding their computational burden, establishing it as a practical approach for domain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: RAEF represents a practical and scalable approach for domain adaptation in time series forecasting that balances performance and efficiency, offering a viable alternative to computationally expensive fine-tuning methods.

title: HELIX: Model-Harness Co-evolution for Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Scaling agent capability has largely focused on improving the model, yet an interactive agent acts through a runtime harness that mediates context, tools, control flow, and stopping. The harness shapes both what a model can accomplish and the trajectories from which it learns. This coupling motivates model-harness co-evolution for recursive self-improvement: build harnesses for a fixed model, update the model from verified sibling trajectories, and rebuild the harnesses as model capabilities change. Realizing this loop requires a controlled way to evolve harnesses while preserving intervention identity and effect. We present HELIX, a source-traceable substrate for harness evolution. HELIX decomposes agent systems into typed ports, reusable atoms, recipes, product shells, and runtime policies. It makes interventions explicit and auditable while retaining trajectories, test outcomes, and provenance. Harness evolution thus serves two linked roles: improving fixed-model execution and producing matched successes, regressions, near misses, and alternative solutions as data for subsequent model improvement. We evaluate HELIX in one evolution round on code repair. A 65-candidate portfolio discovers a fixed harness that improves task coverage by 4.0% over Pi, while the full portfolio exposes up to 58.0% more verified coverage through complementary sibling behavior. Selected candidates are assessed with repeated runs and the SWE-bench evaluator. A 200-slot sibling slice yields 438 verified SFT, critic, filter, and preference records. These results show how harness, model, and data form a feedback system: harness evolution expands current capability and creates learning signal for the next model; model updates motivate the next round of harness evolution. HELIX provides an auditable interface for studying this recursive process. Code is available at https://github.com/HKUDS/HELIX.

AI.tldr: HELIX is a source-traceable system for evolving agent runtime harnesses that enables model-harness co-evolution for recursive self-improvement through explicit interventions and auditable trajectories.
AI.motivation: Current agent scaling focuses mainly on improving models, but runtime harnesses (which mediate context, tools, control flow, and stopping) are equally important as they shape what models can accomplish and the trajectories they learn from. This coupling motivates model-harness co-evolution for recursive self-improvement.
AI.method: HELIX decomposes agent systems into typed ports, reusable atoms, recipes, product shells, and runtime policies. It makes interventions explicit and auditable while preserving trajectories, test outcomes, and provenance. The system enables controlled harness evolution that preserves intervention identity and effect.
AI.result: In code repair evaluation: a 65-candidate portfolio discovered a fixed harness that improved task coverage by 4.0% over Pi, while the full portfolio exposed up to 58.0% more verified coverage through complementary sibling behavior. A 200-slot sibling slice yielded 438 verified SFT, critic, filter, and preference records.
AI.conclusion: Harness, model, and data form a feedback system: harness evolution expands current capability and creates learning signals for the next model, while model updates motivate subsequent harness evolution. HELIX provides an auditable interface for studying this recursive co-evolution process.

title: When Denoising Hurts: Rethinking the Terminal Step of Diffusion Time Series Forecasters -- Extended Version
summary: Diffusion models offer a natural way to model uncertainty in time series forecasting, yet their iterative sampling process is often treated as a uniformly beneficial refinement procedure. Our study challenges this view by examining how forecast quality evolves throughout reverse diffusion. We find that general temporal structure is often recovered at relatively high noise levels, whereas continued low-noise refinement can introduce statistical drift and degrade the final forecast. Our analysis further suggests that this behavior explains why prior methods often favor relatively narrow diffusion architecture and schedule design. Building on this observation, we propose a label-free global stopping criterion that detects the optimal termination point, eventually speeding up inference and improving predictive accuracy. Additionally, since early stopping terminates inference in high-noise regions, we propose a Bernoulli timestep sampler that concentrates training on this region while preserving coverage of the full diffusion process. Extensive experiments conducted across eight real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: Diffusion models for time series forecasting don't always benefit from full reverse diffusion; early stopping at the right noise level improves both speed and accuracy, with a Bernoulli sampler to focus training on relevant regions.
AI.motivation: While diffusion models naturally handle uncertainty in time series forecasting, the common assumption that iterative sampling is uniformly beneficial throughout reverse diffusion may be flawed. The paper aims to understand how forecast quality actually evolves during the diffusion process and improve upon existing methods.
AI.method: 1. Analyze forecast quality evolution throughout reverse diffusion, discovering that general temporal structure is recovered at high noise levels while low-noise refinement can cause drift; 2. Propose a label-free global stopping criterion to detect optimal termination point; 3. Introduce a Bernoulli timestep sampler that concentrates training on high-noise regions while maintaining full process coverage.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across eight real-world datasets demonstrate superior performance compared to existing approaches, with improved predictive accuracy and faster inference through optimal early stopping.
AI.conclusion: Reverse diffusion isn't uniformly beneficial for time series forecasting - early stopping at appropriate noise levels is optimal. The proposed stopping criterion and Bernoulli sampler provide practical improvements in both efficiency and accuracy, explaining why prior methods favored certain architecture and schedule designs.

title: Implementing Computational Law in Wolfram Language for the Governance of Artificial Intelligence
comment: 25 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables, 12 code listings. Wolfram Language implementation and verification script (31 assertions) available at https://github.com/Zaffer/research-computational-law
summary: How do we govern AI systems whose reasoning we cannot fully inspect? Governance does not require understanding a system's reasoning. It requires stating what the system is obliged, permitted, and forbidden to do, and checking whether it complied. I present an implementation of Reified Input/Output Logic, the formalism behind the DAPRECO knowledge base, in Wolfram Language: the core I/O axioms, obligations, permissions, constitutive norms, reified eventualities, and temporal operators. I then test whether GPT-4 can translate English legal statements into the formalism, and report the failures: hallucinated functions, omitted temporal scope, deviation from the formalism, and (in the worst cases) code that runs, reads plausibly, but silently encodes the wrong norm. A case study, an AI guard dog operating under a computational contract, shows how formalized rules can extend from a contract directly into the operational code of an embodied agent, producing symbolic, auditable justifications for its behaviour. I argue that computational law can be used as a governance tool and that a desirable goal would be to formalize the law that can and ought to be programmatically executable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Reified Input/Output Logic (implemented in Wolfram Language) as a governance tool for AI systems, allowing formal specification of obligations, permissions, and prohibitions without needing to understand the system's internal reasoning.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of governing AI systems whose internal reasoning processes are opaque or not fully inspectable. Governance needs to ensure AI systems behave appropriately even when we cannot understand how they reach decisions.
AI.method: The author implements Reified Input/Output Logic in Wolfram Language, creating a formal framework for expressing norms (obligations, permissions, constitutive norms). They test GPT-4's ability to translate English legal statements into this formalism and identify common failure modes.
AI.result: GPT-4 struggles with accurate translation: it hallucinates functions, omits temporal scope, deviates from the formalism, and sometimes produces code that runs but encodes incorrect norms. A case study shows how formalized rules can extend from contracts directly into embodied AI agents' operational code.
AI.conclusion: Computational law can serve as a governance tool for AI systems. The desirable goal should be to formalize laws that can and should be programmatically executable, enabling symbolic, auditable justifications for AI behavior through computational contracts.

title: Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning for One-Warehouse Multi-Store Systems with Censored Demand
summary: The one-warehouse multi-store (OWMS) system is a fundamental inventory network in which a nonreplenishable warehouse allocates shared stock across multiple stores over time. Existing OWMS learning policies are built around a fixed target calibrated to the initial average resource rate, but such a fixed-target architecture cannot re-center after realized sales change the remaining resource available per future period. We develop Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning, a new learning framework that tracks the primal-dual resolving path with censored demand as the remaining-resource state evolves. In each period, the current resource rate indexes the target store allocations and dual variable, while censored sales provide gradient estimates for updating both. The analysis combines expected-sales geometry with a moving-target argument to yield logarithmic expected regret, improving on the state-of-the-art square-root-order guarantees of existing OWMS learning policies. The underlying design and analytical ideas may inform other online learning problems with depleting shared resources. Numerical experiments further demonstrate good finite-horizon performance of a practical variant across different horizon lengths and inventory regimes.

AI.tldr: New learning framework for OWMS inventory systems that adapts to changing resource availability, achieving logarithmic regret vs. existing square-root guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing OWMS learning policies use fixed targets based on initial resource rates, but cannot adapt when realized sales change remaining resources per period. Need dynamic adaptation.
AI.method: Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning framework that tracks primal-dual resolving path with censored demand. Uses current resource rate to index target allocations and dual variables, with censored sales providing gradient estimates for updates.
AI.result: Achieves logarithmic expected regret, improving on state-of-the-art square-root-order guarantees. Numerical experiments show good finite-horizon performance across different horizon lengths and inventory regimes.
AI.conclusion: Proposed adaptive learning framework significantly improves regret guarantees for OWMS systems. Design and analytical ideas may inform other online learning problems with depleting shared resources.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B on Apple Silicon: Fixing Deployment Bugs and Decreasing Looped Transformer Memory Overhead
comment: 8 pages, 3 Tables
summary: Nanbeige4.2-3B is a 3B-parameter agentic model built around a Looped Transformer (LT) that reuses one stack of layers for a second forward pass, adding effective depth without additional parameters. Evaluated on Apple Silicon (MPS), we identify five independent bugs which prevent the released checkpoint from running via Hugging Face transformers out of the box (including a silently-zeroed RoPE buffer and calls to removed transformers cache APIs). Furthermore, we show that fixing these bugs is still not sufficient for agentic tasks, due to the LT's layer-reuse strategy (which effectively doubles peak attention memory) used to achieve parameter efficiency. We thus introduce a chunked-prefill strategy which alleviates the incurred memory-capacity penalty, extending allowable context width by $2.7 \times$ on 32~GiB shared memory. However, even with the reduced memory overhead, we show that patches are required to render Nanbeige4.2-3B usable; resolving both system prompt and MPS-native memory bugs finally allows reliable evaluation on standard MCP and tool-calling benchmarks. On a subset of MCPMark, the debugged model completes up to 30\% of real agentic tasks (up from the original's 0\%), while, on BFCL, it is near-perfect at single tool calls (yet fails the majority of multi-tool tests). We release the patched checkpoint, system prompt optimizer, and evaluation harnesses at https://github.com/johnhalloran321/Nanbeige4.2-3B-mps-fix.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and fixes critical bugs in Nanbeige4.2-3B, a 3B-parameter agentic model, making it usable on Apple Silicon while addressing memory inefficiencies from its looped transformer architecture.
AI.motivation: The original Nanbeige4.2-3B model has serious implementation bugs that prevent it from running on Apple Silicon via Hugging Face transformers, and its looped transformer architecture causes memory inefficiencies that hinder agentic task performance.
AI.method: 1) Identified five independent bugs in the original implementation (including RoPE buffer issues and removed cache APIs). 2) Developed chunked-prefill strategy to reduce memory overhead from looped transformer's layer reuse. 3) Fixed system prompt and MPS-native memory bugs to enable reliable evaluation.
