AI.result: The patched model now completes up to 30% of real agentic tasks on MCPMark (from original's 0%), achieves near-perfect performance on single tool calls in BFCL, but still fails most multi-tool tests. Memory improvements allow 2.7× longer context windows on 32GiB shared memory.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully debugs and optimizes Nanbeige4.2-3B for Apple Silicon, releasing patched checkpoints and tools that make the model usable for agentic tasks while highlighting remaining challenges with multi-tool coordination.

title: Sequence prediction under a lying oracle
summary: We consider the problem of sequential prediction of an $m$-ary sequence, where at each epoch, (i) the environment selects an outcome from an $m$-ary alphabet, (ii) the learner selects a probability distribution over the same alphabet (unaware of the outcome generated by the environment), and finally, (iii) the learner incurs a cost that depends on the probability assigned to the outcome. The cost function we consider captures the complexity of predicting the outcome generated by the environment, in a scenario where the aforementioned prediction is performed via comparative queries to a lying oracle. We consider both stochastic and adversarial environments, propose algorithms for both settings, and establish logarithmic upper bounds on their regret.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes algorithms for sequential prediction of m-ary sequences using comparative queries to a lying oracle, with logarithmic regret bounds for both stochastic and adversarial environments.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of predicting outcomes in sequential prediction tasks where predictions are made via comparative queries to a potentially lying oracle. This captures realistic scenarios where prediction mechanisms involve querying systems that may provide inaccurate responses.
AI.method: The authors propose algorithms for both stochastic and adversarial environments. The approach involves sequential prediction where: (1) environment selects an outcome from m-ary alphabet, (2) learner selects a probability distribution, (3) learner incurs cost based on assigned probability to the actual outcome. The algorithms specifically handle prediction via comparative queries to a lying oracle.
AI.result: The paper establishes logarithmic upper bounds on regret for both stochastic and adversarial settings. This means the proposed algorithms achieve near-optimal performance with regret growing only logarithmically with time.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithms effectively handle sequential prediction tasks involving comparative queries to lying oracles, achieving efficient logarithmic regret bounds that work well in both stochastic and adversarial environments.

title: Content Depth Matters in Short-Video Recommendation: Rethinking the Attention Economy
comment: 9 Pages
summary: Driven by the attention economy, short-video Recommender Systems (RSs) are primarily optimized to maximize user engagement by promoting videos that capture attention within seconds. These systems inherently favor shallow-content videos that are effective at attracting immediate attention. However, growing evidence suggests that prolonged exposure to such content may negatively affect users' cognitive engagement and mental well-being, raising concerns about the long-term societal impact of the short-video platform. To tackle this challenge, this paper introduces a new metric, the \textbf{Content Depth Score (CDS)}, to quantify the content depth of short videos. CDS measures the extent to which a video is expected to stimulate higher-order cognitive processes, using a seven-level scale grounded in established theories of cognitive psychology and learning. As an initial step toward this vision, we present \textbf{SCOPE-Bench}, the first benchmark for content-depth evaluation in short-video recommendation. Built upon a large-scale open-source short-video dataset, SCOPE-Bench provides CDS annotations for 150K videos, enabling systematic evaluation of RSs from a cognitive-content perspective. Leveraging SCOPE-Bench, we evaluate 13 representative RSs and reveal a consistent preference for shallow-content videos. Moreover, we find that these algorithms recommending cognitively deep content are only marginally better than random selection, highlighting a previously overlooked limitation of existing recommendation objectives. Our code and datasets are available at https://liweidengdavid.github.io/SCOPE-Bench/.

AI.tldr: A benchmark called SCOPE-Bench introduces Content Depth Score (CDS) to evaluate short-video recommendation systems beyond engagement metrics, revealing they favor shallow content and perform poorly at recommending cognitively deep videos.
AI.motivation: Current short-video recommender systems are optimized for engagement metrics, which favor attention-grabbing but shallow content. This raises concerns about negative long-term impacts on users' cognitive engagement and mental well-being, creating a need to evaluate and improve recommendation quality from a cognitive perspective.
AI.method: Introduced Content Depth Score (CDS), a metric based on cognitive psychology theories using a seven-level scale to quantify content depth. Created SCOPE-Bench, the first benchmark with CDS annotations for 150K videos from a large-scale dataset. Evaluated 13 representative recommendation systems using this benchmark.
AI.result: The evaluation revealed that current recommender systems consistently prefer shallow-content videos. More critically, these algorithms perform only marginally better than random selection when it comes to recommending cognitively deep content, exposing a fundamental limitation of existing recommendation objectives.
AI.conclusion: The research highlights a critical gap in short-video recommendation systems: they prioritize immediate engagement over cognitive depth. SCOPE-Bench provides a valuable tool for evaluating and improving recommendation quality from a cognitive perspective, suggesting future systems should consider content depth as an important quality dimension beyond engagement metrics.

title: Forecast Collapse in Time-Series Foundation Models
comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/abel-lab/finance1k
summary: When forecasting hourly returns for 1,000 US equities, we observe an unexpected phenomenon: predictions become nearly flat and show poor stock ranking, as measured by cross-sectional correlation. We call this forecast collapse. Surprisingly, the phenomenon largely disappears when forecasting trading volume under the same setting. We investigate forecast collapse across time-series foundation models (TSFMs), twelve deep-learning forecasting models, and 97 public benchmark configurations, and find that it is closely tied to target predictability. We identify two distinct reasons behind it: low predictability limits the amplitude of calibrated point forecasts, while per-series objectives leave cross-series structure unidentified. These findings reveal a calibration-ranking tradeoff: optimizing squared error leads to flat predictions, whereas directly optimizing cross-sectional correlation improves ranking but can inflate forecast amplitude by more than an order of magnitude. To address this tradeoff, we introduce CalibRank, a simple objective that balances calibration and ranking. On Finance1K, CalibRank nearly triples cross-sectional correlation while keeping amplitude close to the target, and improves correlation on all tested models. Our results reveal a blind spot in conventional time-series evaluation: per-series metrics can hide failures in cross-series structure needed by downstream decisions.

AI.tldr: When forecasting hourly stock returns, predictions become flat and rank stocks poorly (forecast collapse), but this doesn't happen with trading volume. The paper identifies a calibration-ranking tradeoff and introduces CalibRank to balance both.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the unexpected phenomenon of "forecast collapse" where hourly equity return predictions become nearly flat and show poor cross-sectional ranking ability, despite the same models working well for trading volume forecasting.
AI.method: The authors investigate forecast collapse across time-series foundation models, twelve deep-learning forecasting models, and 97 public benchmark configurations. They identify two causes: low predictability limits forecast amplitude, and per-series objectives fail to capture cross-series structure. They introduce CalibRank, a new objective that balances calibration and ranking.
AI.result: CalibRank nearly triples cross-sectional correlation while keeping forecast amplitude close to the target on Finance1K dataset. It improves correlation across all tested models, addressing the calibration-ranking tradeoff where optimizing squared error leads to flat predictions while optimizing correlation inflates amplitude excessively.
AI.conclusion: The paper reveals a blind spot in conventional time-series evaluation: per-series metrics can hide failures in cross-series structure needed for downstream decisions. The proposed CalibRank effectively balances calibration and ranking, solving the forecast collapse problem for financial return predictions.

title: Simulation-Driven Vehicular Traffic Data Augmentation: Extending Sensor Coverage Through Virtual Sensing
summary: Urban traffic management relies on sensor networks whose spatial coverage is limited by deployment costs and privacy regulations. Machine learning models trained on such sparse data cannot generalize to unmonitored locations and must be retrained whenever the sensor infrastructure changes. We propose a simulation-based methodology that addresses this problem by generating augmented traffic count datasets in which each physical sensor is replaced by a virtual sensor placed at a surrogate location in the road network. Virtual sensors are selected by a graph-search heuristic that jointly maximises vehicle-flow continuity and traffic-metric similarity between the original and surrogate locations, while enforcing a minimum spatial displacement to ensure diversity of observed traffic conditions. We validate the method on two Belgian cities: Brussels, using a calibrated model, and Namur, using synthetic models. The augmented datasets preserve the bimodal daily demand profile and the dynamics of traffic at the observed locations.

AI.tldr: A simulation-based method to generate augmented traffic data by replacing physical sensors with virtual sensors at surrogate locations, enabling better generalization of ML models without requiring new physical sensors.
AI.motivation: Urban traffic management has limited sensor coverage due to deployment costs and privacy regulations. ML models trained on sparse sensor data fail to generalize to unmonitored locations and need retraining when sensor infrastructure changes.
AI.method: Uses simulation-based methodology to generate augmented traffic datasets where each physical sensor is replaced by a virtual sensor at a surrogate location. Virtual sensors are selected via graph-search heuristic that maximizes vehicle-flow continuity and traffic-metric similarity while enforcing minimum spatial displacement for diversity.
AI.result: Validated on two Belgian cities (Brussels with calibrated model, Namur with synthetic models). Augmented datasets preserve the bimodal daily demand profile and traffic dynamics at observed locations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed simulation-based virtual sensor approach effectively addresses sensor sparsity in urban traffic management, enabling creation of diverse traffic datasets that maintain key traffic characteristics without requiring additional physical infrastructure.

title: Learning to Run Power Networks: Effective AlphaZero-inspired Topological Control
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in ACM SIGENERGY Energy Informatics Review, Volume 6, Issue 3, September 2026
summary: As the integration of volatile renewable energy sources increases the strain on modern power grids, the use of Reinforcement Learning (RL) for autonomous topological reconfiguration has emerged as a promising research field to keep strained grids stable and operational. Compared to traditional redispatching measures, topological actions offer a cheaper and more cost-effective way to manage grid congestion. However, their implementation is hindered by a vast combinatorial action space and strict operational constraints. This paper investigates the effectiveness of model-based AlphaZero-inspired approaches that utilize Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for proactive grid management. We systematically evaluate how reward functions, observation density, and search guidance influence an agent's survivability. Our results demonstrate that the optimized AlphaZero approach achieves a peak survivability of 98.43%, significantly outperforming the proximal policy optimization (PPO) variant. We find that conducting the MCTS without guidance from a prior learned policy or value function can enhance training efficiency, and that a straightforward binary survival reward provides more effective search guidance than complex, multi-objective functions. Our findings demonstrate that while AlphaZero is a powerful framework for topological control, pure reinforcement learning is not sufficient; rather, an effective and reliable system requires a 'minimalist' integration of domain-specific heuristics, binary rewards, and a restricted observation space of line loads.

AI.tldr: AlphaZero with Monte Carlo Tree Search outperforms PPO for power grid topological reconfiguration, achieving 98.43% survivability using minimalist design: domain heuristics, binary rewards, and limited observation space.
AI.motivation: The increasing integration of volatile renewable energy sources strains modern power grids, requiring autonomous topological reconfiguration to maintain stability. Traditional redispatching measures are costly, while topological actions offer cheaper congestion management, but face challenges from vast combinatorial action spaces and strict operational constraints.
AI.method: The paper investigates model-based AlphaZero-inspired approaches using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for proactive grid management. It systematically evaluates reward functions, observation density, and search guidance influences on agent survivability. The approach uses a minimalist integration of domain-specific heuristics, binary survival rewards, and restricted observation space of line loads.

MCTS without guidance from learned policy/value functions enhances training efficiency. Simple binary survival reward provides more effective search guidance than complex multi-objective functions.
AI.conclusion: AlphaZero is a powerful framework for topological control, but pure reinforcement learning is insufficient. An effective system requires minimalist integration of domain heuristics, binary rewards, and restricted observation space. The study demonstrates practical feasibility of RL-based topological control while identifying key design principles for success.

title: Buy the Rumor, Sell the News: When Is News Priced In?
summary: Two old market sayings hold that news is already priced in by the time it is published, and that the rumor is bought while the news is sold. Both place the price move associated with a piece of news before and at publication rather than after it. Whether the claims hold, for which kinds of news, and by how much are basic questions about how fast markets absorb public information. We test them on 4.57 million financial news articles covering roughly 3,000 US stocks (2023-2026). A large language model teacher, distilled into a compact classifier through active learning, assigns each article one of 17 event tags and five attributes; articles are clustered into stories to separate first reports from follow-up coverage; and beta-adjusted abnormal returns are measured around the resulting 1.68 million stock-day events, with 364,405 neutral-sentiment events as a placebo group. Three results follow. First, the price move associated with news concentrates before and at publication: pooled across all signed events, the cumulative move in the news direction by the close of publication day is 2.8 times its value 20 days later, and for rumor-flagged events the rumor day captures the entire move while the subsequent confirmation contributes nothing. Second, measured against the placebo of comparable stocks, markets underreact to numbers and overreact to stories: quantified fundamental news (earnings, dividends, guidance, analyst actions) keeps drifting in the direction of the news for weeks, while soft story-driven news (launches, macro commentary, leadership) gives back its move. Third, news carries width as well as direction: publicity raises volatility before the publication day, and volatility declines once the news is out, because publication resolves uncertainty. The study also produces a table of measured drift for each event tag, usable as a prior in news-conditioned forecasting models.

AI.tldr: Financial news moves prices mostly BEFORE publication; markets underreact to hard numbers but overreact to soft stories, with volatility peaking before news release then declining.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether two classic market sayings hold true: "news is already priced in" and "buy the rumor, sell the news." These sayings suggest price moves happen before news publication. The authors want to test how quickly markets absorb public information for different types of news, using modern computational methods on a large dataset.
AI.method: Researchers analyzed 4.57 million financial news articles covering ~3,000 US stocks (2023-2026). They used a large language model teacher distilled into a compact classifier through active learning to categorize articles into 17 event types and 5 attributes. Articles were clustered into stories to separate first reports from follow-up coverage. The study measured beta-adjusted abnormal returns around 1.68 million stock-day events, using 364,405 neutral-sentiment events as a placebo control group for comparison.
AI.result: Three key findings: 1) Price moves concentrate before/at publication - the cumulative move by publication close is 2.8x its value 20 days later, with rumor days capturing entire moves. 2) Markets underreact to quantitative fundamental news (earnings, dividends, guidance, analyst actions) but overreact to soft story-driven news (launches, macro commentary, leadership). 3) News affects volatility too - publicity raises volatility before publication, then declines after as uncertainty resolves. The study also provides a table of measured drift for each event type for forecasting models.
AI.conclusion: Traditional market wisdom about news timing largely holds - price moves indeed concentrate around publication. However, market reactions vary systematically by news type: quantitative news shows underreaction (post-announcement drift), while qualitative news shows overreaction (price reversal). This distinction between "numbers" and "stories" provides a framework for understanding news-driven market efficiency.

title: From Fixed Grids to Moving Particles:A Transferable Latent Operator for Fluid Dynamics
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures.Preprint
summary: Lagrangian modeling is vital to fluid dynamics, as it characterizes particle transport and complements the Eulerian description.However, Lagrangian trajectories are less commonly available than Eulerian fields, while most neural operators are trained and evaluated primarily in the Eulerian representation. This mismatch motivates a new learning problem: can a model trained solely on Eulerian observations generalize zero-shot from Eulerian field prediction to Lagrangian particle rollout, without Lagrangian supervision or task-specific adaptation? To address this problem, we propose the Transferable Latent Operator (TLO), which learns a unified flow representation shared by Eulerian field prediction and Lagrangian particle rollout. TLO decouples latent flow evolution from coordinate-dependent decoding: querying the evolving latent representation at fixed spatial coordinates yields Eulerian fields, whereas querying velocities at particle positions and recursively updating these positions enables Lagrangian rollout. Across five fluid-dynamics benchmarks, TLO consistently outperforms existing neural operators in both Eulerian field prediction and zero-shot Lagrangian rollout, with further gains from limited Lagrangian fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: TLO learns unified flow representations enabling zero-shot generalization from Eulerian field prediction to Lagrangian particle rollout without Lagrangian supervision.
AI.motivation: Lagrangian trajectories are less available than Eulerian fields, creating a mismatch with neural operators trained primarily on Eulerian data. There's a need for models that can generalize from Eulerian observations to Lagrangian particle rollout without Lagrangian supervision or task-specific adaptation.
AI.method: Proposes Transferable Latent Operator (TLO) that learns a unified flow representation shared by both Eulerian field prediction and Lagrangian particle rollout. TLO decouples latent flow evolution from coordinate-dependent decoding: querying latent representation at fixed coordinates yields Eulerian fields, while querying velocities at particle positions with recursive position updates enables Lagrangian rollout.
AI.result: TLO consistently outperforms existing neural operators across five fluid-dynamics benchmarks in both Eulerian field prediction and zero-shot Lagrangian rollout, with further improvements from limited Lagrangian fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The TLO approach successfully addresses the learning problem of generalizing from Eulerian observations to Lagrangian particle rollout without Lagrangian supervision, demonstrating the effectiveness of unified flow representations for fluid dynamics modeling.

title: Residual Dominance as a Structural Account of Last-Item Reliance in Causal Self-Attention Recommenders
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys'26)
summary: Transformer-based sequential recommenders with causal self-attention often rely heavily on the most recent interaction at inference time, but how this behavior is structurally expressed in the representation used for prediction remains unclear. We combine prediction-time diagnostics with norm-based analysis of the full attention block. First, we show that SASRec-style models exhibit highly localized last-item reliance. We then find that, although self-attention aggregates contextual information, residual addition sharply shifts the full-block representation toward same-position contributions, which we term residual dominance. To probe this interpretation, we use inference-time residual scaling as a controlled diagnostic intervention. Changing the residual strength induces a monotonic trade-off between structural mixing and last-item reliance, while reducing residual strength recovers a subset of final-position misses for which representations at non-final positions already rank the ground-truth item correctly. Our results provide a structural account linking extreme last-item reliance to residual dominance at inference time. The code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: Transformer-based sequential recommenders heavily rely on the last item at inference due to residual dominance in the attention block, where residual addition shifts representations toward same-position contributions rather than contextual mixing.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based sequential recommenders with causal self-attention often rely heavily on the most recent interaction at inference time, but how this behavior is structurally expressed in the representation used for prediction remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors combine prediction-time diagnostics with norm-based analysis of the full attention block. They use inference-time residual scaling as a controlled diagnostic intervention to probe the structural behavior.
AI.result:
1) SASRec-style models exhibit highly localized last-item reliance.
2) Self-attention aggregates contextual information but residual addition sharply shifts the full-block representation toward same-position contributions (termed residual dominance).
3) Inference-time residual scaling induces a monotonic trade-off between structural mixing and last-item reliance.
4) Reducing residual strength recovers a subset of final-position misses where non-final positions already rank the ground-truth item correctly.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that extreme last-item reliance in SASRec-style models can be structurally explained by residual dominance at inference time. The results provide a clearer understanding of how causal self-attention mechanisms in transformers for sequential recommendation actually operate during prediction.

title: Overcoming Shortcut Learning in Graph Neural Networks through Active Explanation Guidance
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can solve prediction tasks by unintentionally exploiting shortcuts---that is, edges, nodes, and features that correlate with but are not causal for the prediction---which compromise their reliability in out-of-distribution tasks. We introduce XIGL, an architecture-agnostic human-in-the-loop strategy for removing such shortcuts from GNNs. Our key insight is twofold. On the one hand, reliance on shortcuts can be detected by inspecting GNN explanations. On the other hand, once made aware of such shortcuts, sufficiently expert users can provide tailored corrective feedback, which helps deconfound the model. XIGL supports any query strategy; however, since corrective feedback can be expensive to acquire, we develop an active learning strategy for prioritizing explanations that are more likely to display shortcut behavior, lowering annotation and cognitive costs. We showcase the effectiveness of XIGL, including both existing and proposed explanation-based strategies, on several GNN architectures. Our implementation is available online.

AI.tldr: XIGL: A human-in-the-loop strategy that uses GNN explanations to detect and remove shortcut reliance in graph neural networks through expert corrective feedback.
AI.motivation: GNNs can unintentionally exploit shortcuts (edges, nodes, and features correlated with but not causal for predictions), compromising reliability in out-of-distribution tasks.
AI.method: XIGL is an architecture-agnostic strategy that: 1) detects shortcut reliance by inspecting GNN explanations, 2) uses expert users to provide tailored corrective feedback to deconfound the model, and 3) includes an active learning strategy to prioritize explanations likely to display shortcut behavior, reducing annotation costs.
AI.result: XIGL effectively removes shortcut reliance from GNNs, works across multiple GNN architectures, and the active learning strategy lowers annotation and cognitive costs.
AI.conclusion: XIGL provides a practical human-in-the-loop approach to improve GNN reliability by detecting and removing shortcut exploitation through explanation-guided expert feedback, with implementation available online.
